Superpowers skills override default system prompt behavior, but **user instructions always take precedence**:

## How to Access Skills

**In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and presented to youâ€”follow it directly. Never use the Read tool on skill files.

**In Copilot CLI:** Use the `skill` tool. Skills are auto-discovered from installed plugins. The `skill` tool works the same as Claude Code's `Skill` tool.

**In Gemini CLI:** Skills activate via the `activate_skill` tool. Gemini loads skill metadata at session start and activates the full content on demand.

**In other environments:** Check your platform's documentation for how skills are loaded.

## Platform Adaptation

# Using Skills

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action.** Even a 1% chance a skill might apply means that you should invoke the skill to check. If an invoked skill turns out to be wrong for the situation, you don't need to use it.

## Red Flags

"Let's build X" â†’ brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
"Fix this bug" â†’ debugging first, then domain-specific skills.

1. What recent JNT papers actually look like
I treated â€œrecentâ€ as approximately 2021â€“2026 and compared the manuscript with a cross-section of papers published or accepted in JNT: short classical-number-theory papers, medium-length analytic and probabilistic papers, and at least one article exceeding forty pages. The relevant comparison set includes Browningâ€“Shparlinski on square-free polynomial values, Chowâ€“Jones on the Fibonacci partition function, Liâ€“Wangâ€“Wangâ€“Yi on covering systems, Granthamâ€“Granville on primes in recurrence sequences, and recent longer papers on Iwasawa modules and random characteristic polynomials. The journal accepts a broad range of authorial styles, so there is no rigid template, but there is a recognizable editorial register. arXiv+4ç§‘å­¦ç›´é€šè½¦+4arXiv+4
How a typical paper opens
A normal JNT paper opens by putting a familiar arithmetic object or problem on the page immediately. It then gives enough history to locate the precise question, formulates the new result, and moves into proofs. The opening is usually problem-driven rather than manifesto-driven.
The main theorem commonly appears on pages 2â€“4. It need not be on the first page. Browningâ€“Shparlinski first state the square-free-value problem, describe the earlier range, define the family being averaged, and then give Theorem 1.1. Chowâ€“Jones introduce the Fibonacci partition function, explain the misleading naÃ¯ve prediction, show the numerical phenomenon, and state Theorem 1.1 on the third preprint page. The covering-systems paper gives a somewhat longer history and the necessary function-field definitions before stating its main theorem near the end of the introduction. Thus JNT readily permits either â€œproblem, history, theoremâ€ or â€œproblem, example/computation, theorem,â€ but it does not normally postpone the result until after a general essay on the paperâ€™s architecture. arXiv arXiv arXiv
For an ordinary 15â€“30-page paper, the introduction is often roughly 8â€“15% of the article. It may rise toward 15â€“20% when substantial history, examples, or conjectural heuristics are essential. In a forty- or fifty-page article, an introduction of five or six pages is not itself abnormal. The deciding question is whether those pages create a hierarchy or merely inventory everything that follows.
Your introduction occupies a little over six pages before Section 2 starts, so approximately 12% of the 52-page main article. The proportion is normal for JNT. The density and function of those pages are not.
How much explanatory prose is normal
Recent JNT papers are not austere lemma warehouses. Authors commonly give:


one or two paragraphs at the beginning of a section explaining the next mathematical move;


a sentence before a proposition explaining why it is needed;


a brief observation inside a proof when a construction changes direction;


a remark after a result when there is a genuine arithmetic consequence, limitation, or comparison.


But the body remains theorem-proof dominated. As a rough reading impression rather than a measured journal statistic, perhaps two-thirds to three-quarters of a conventional JNT body consists of definitions, estimates, formal arguments, and proofs. Explanatory prose is concentrated at points of transition. It is not repeated before and after each theorem.
Chowâ€“Jones are a useful close comparator. Their introduction gives motivation and numerical evidence, but once the proof begins, the prose is local and operational: a case is introduced because it must be counted, a recurrence is motivated because the previous count produces it, and the proof proceeds. Browningâ€“Shparlinski similarly give substantial contextual prose in the introduction, then move to compact preliminaries and sustained technical work. arXiv arXiv
How proofs are written
A short proof that delegates its substance to an existing theorem is entirely acceptable in JNT when the result really is an immediate application, a standard estimate, or a change of conventions. Browningâ€“Shparlinski, for example, prove one preliminary bound by referring directly to Stewart, Lagrangeâ€™s theorem, and Henselâ€™s lemma. arXiv
But the journal expects the article to carry the argument at precisely those points where the authors claim a new translation, endpoint treatment, arithmetic normalization, or strengthening. â€œApply [X]â€ is not enough when the contribution consists in showing that [X] applies with different indexing or at a previously excluded endpoint. Conversely, once such a transfer has been verified, JNT does not reward reproducing every branch of the source theory merely to demonstrate thoroughness.
Routine verifications are normally handled in one of three ways:


a sentence inside the proof;


a short lemma when the fact will be reused materially;


an appendix only when the computation is lengthy and genuinely distracts from the principal argument.


A formally named theorem whose proof is â€œthis is exactly the preceding corollaryâ€ is not the usual register. Nor is a succession of formally named statements each memorializing one stage of the authorsâ€™ checking process.
Appendices and supplementary material
The dominant custom in the recent JNT papers I examined is to carry the mathematical article in one document. Many have no appendix at all. Browningâ€“Shparlinskiâ€™s table of contents runs directly from the introduction through preliminaries, technical sections, proofs, and references. The accepted covering-systems paper similarly has three main sections and no appended second article. Chowâ€“Jones is essentially introduction, the main counting argument, recurrence solution, references. arXiv arXiv arXiv
My practical estimate of the house custom is:


0â€“10% appended material: entirely ordinary;


10â€“20%: noticeable but acceptable when it consists of computations, data, technical uniformity lemmas, or convention-heavy checks;


about 27%, as in a 52-page main article plus a 19-page supplement: distinctly unusual.


The issue is not a formal prohibition. It is that a supplement of that size often signals one of two editorial problems: either essential proof material has been displaced from the paper, or the package contains a second paper that has not been separated.
The uploaded object contains only the 52-page main article; it ends with the references and author addresses on page 52. The supplement is described in the article as containing â€œconditional arithmetic and integer moment consequences,â€ and later as containing â€œconditional microcanonical, dyadic-ray, and integer-moment consequences outside the main theorem spine,â€ but the supplement itself is not attached. I can therefore assess the 52:19 architecture and the categories named by the authors, but not the supplementâ€™s paragraph-level style or internal organization.   
Prose register
First-person plural is normal: â€œwe prove,â€ â€œwe shall use,â€ â€œwe now apply.â€ Impersonal constructions also occur, but JNT does not expect a forced passive voice. Results are referred to by number. A section opening may remind the reader of the preceding result and state the next objective. Motivation is repeated only when the mathematical perspective genuinely changes.
The register is confident but not promotional. Authors do not usually keep an account, throughout the paper, of which sentence is imported, which result is a transfer, which claim is not being made, which adjacent manuscript does what, and which possible theorem remains open. That information belongs principally in one well-written passage in the introduction and, where necessary, in a precise local attribution.
The principal tells of a non-JNT register
The following are the common warning signs:


the introduction reads like an extended abstract plus a response to earlier referees;


every theorem is followed by a miniature proof synopsis;


elementary consequences and major results receive the same ceremonial presentation;


a paper repeatedly assures the reader that it is not claiming things;


an independent second theorem family begins late in the article;


the appendix or supplement is large enough to be another article;


transitions describe the document rather than advancing the mathematics;


the conclusion repeats the contribution inventory already given in the abstract and introduction.


Your manuscript exhibits several of these, despite having a genuinely JNT-like mathematical core.

4. Does it read as machine-assisted?
Yes, in its editorial layer it does.
I do not mean that the mathematics reads fabricated or that the proofs lack mathematical individuality. The affine transfer, the orbit-filling construction, and the critical renewal argument have real internal shape. The machine-assisted impression comes from how the text packages and repeatedly explains them.
The strongest specific signs are these.
Repeated contribution ledgers
The paper gives essentially the same imported-versus-new accounting in:

the second page of the introduction;


subsection 1.4;


Remark 5.14;


the conclusion.


Compare the early distinction between transferred and finite-window information, the full contribution inventory in subsection 1.4, the source audit in Remark 5.14, and the closing inventory.    
A human author usually resolves this anxiety once and then writes the paper. Here, the prose keeps reopening the boundary as though every section must be independently safe against misreading.
Throat-clearing and structural announcements
There are many sentences of the form:


â€œThe following lemma records exactlyâ€¦â€


â€œFor clarity, eventual equality is a separate statementâ€¦â€


â€œWe now show thatâ€¦â€


â€œWe record the direct finite-layer recoveryâ€¦â€

Some of these are useful. In aggregate they create the sense that the text is continually announcing its own procedure instead of simply performing it. The sentence that a pressure statement is â€œretained becauseâ€ its normalization is used later is especially revealing: it sounds like an editorial note left in the published narrative.   
Exhaustive enumeration where selection is needed
The introduction gives four headline theorems, their formulas, proof locations, and proof mechanisms. Subsection 1.4 then enumerates every new item and every imported item. Remark 5.14 repeats the source classification almost result by result.
The issue is not accuracy. The issue is editorial judgment. A journal article should choose which three ideas the reader must carry. This manuscript repeatedly gives the reader all of them.
Flat emphasis
Theorem 3.1, whose proof is the preceding corollary, is presented with the same theorem typography as the affine correspondence. The candidate pressure strip, later superseded by the exact pressure theorem, receives a named theorem and numerical width. A non-solution of an arithmetic interface receives a proposition plus two long remarks. Meanwhile, the genuinely decisive orbit-filling idea appears amid the same sequence of named statements.
The mathematics is uneven, as good mathematics should be. The presentation suppresses that unevenness.
Symmetrical sentence construction
The prose repeatedly uses balanced pairs:

pointwise description/multiset description;


imported pressure/finite-window conclusion;

one-dimensional filling/two-dimensional filling;

Some of this reflects real structure. But the recurrence is strong enough that the prose acquires a templated rhythm.
Overall diagnosis
The manuscript does not read like raw machine output. It reads like a technically serious paper that has been machine-assisted through several rounds of defensive expansion and symmetry-seeking revision. The cure is not cosmetic synonym replacement. It is deletion and hierarchy:

allow minor facts to remain minor;

That would make the authorsâ€™ mathematical voice much more visible.

PART TWO â€” YOU ARE THE REFEREE
Recommendation: Major revisions
To the Editor:
The manuscript studies a finite folding map from binary Fibonacci sums to legal Zeckendorf windows. Its principal results give two exact descriptions of the fibre multiplicities, transfer these descriptions to local multiplicity spectra, identify critical finite-size laws at the freezing point of the associated pressure, and prove a full large-deviation principle by supplying lower bounds at the nonexposed slopes. A marked version yields a joint costâ€“multiplicity rate function with an affine coexistence face.
The subject is appropriate for the Journal of Number Theory. The exact affine correspondence and two-layer identity provide a clear arithmetic entry point, and the orbit-filling argument used to complete the large-deviation lower bound is sufficiently concrete that the probabilistic conclusions remain attached to the underlying Fibonacci arithmetic. The manuscript is also careful about attribution: the known golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution pressure and the established extremal classification are not presented as new.
My recommendation is nevertheless major revision rather than acceptance in the present form.
The central problem is not the amount of technical detail by itself. It is that the article has not chosen a sufficiently strict main spine. It currently reads as a combination of:


an article on exact finite-window correspondences;


an article on local and critical Fibonacci-partition thermodynamics;


an article on one-layer and marked large deviations;


a prospectus for conditional prime-support and active-cutoff questions;


a substantial separate supplement.


The first three topics are mathematically connected, but the manuscript presents each as a nearly autonomous theorem suite. This gives subordinate, transferred, intermediate, and principal results comparable textual weight.
The introduction illustrates the problem. The main results are stated early, which is welcome, but each is accompanied by a proof synopsis and location notice. A later subsection then gives a full contribution boundary, a companion-paper disclaimer, and a section-by-section map. Closely related source and contribution inventories recur in Remark 5.14 and the conclusion.   
Several sections retain material that appears to document the development of the project rather than the final proof architecture. Theorem 5.5 confines the pressure boundary to a numerical strip, but Proposition 5.9 subsequently determines the boundary exactly. Proposition 5.12 formulates a finite-prime-support interface, while the following remark explains in considerable detail why the desired active-cutoff theorem is not proved. These results may be useful elsewhere, but they interrupt the route from the exact finite model to the critical law and full LDP.  
The most serious structural issue is Section 6. After the finite-window LDP and critical law have been proved, the manuscript restates and substantially re-proves analogous results intrinsically for one Fibonacci layer, and then proves a joint marked LDP. The section occupies approximately seven pages and reads as a second paper rather than a short application. Moreover, the joint one-layer theorem is advertised as one of the four principal results despite the finite-window title.  
I would ask the authors to reorganize the article around the following sequence:


exact affine and interval correspondences;


local stabilization and the weighted renewal identity;


pressure normalization at the freezing corner;


critical finite-size law;


orbit-filling proof of the full finite-window LDP.


The transferred extremal classification should be stated but its full convention audit can be placed in an appendix. The long reconstruction of the Weinstein branch formulas should be shortened in the article while retaining a complete proof of the endpoint improvement actually needed. The intermediate transition-strip theorem and compact-operator remark should be deleted or moved. The finite-prime-support interface should be placed in the supplement. Section 6 should be reduced to concise corollaries, or separated from the article.
The prose also requires a substantial editorial pass. The manuscript repeatedly uses contribution disclaimers, structure announcements, and statements that explain why another statement is being retained. The result is unusually defensive and gives an impression of machine-assisted uniformity. The authors should state the contribution boundary once in the introduction, retain exact local citations, and remove the repeated audits from the abstract, Remark 5.14, and conclusion.
The stated 52-page article with a 19-page supplement is also outside the usual balance for this journal. I have been supplied only the main article, so I cannot assess the supplement internally. On the description in the main text, however, the conditional arithmetic and integer-moment consequences appear nonessential to the main theorem chain. They should remain separate, and if they constitute a substantial coherent article they should not be presented as a nineteen-page supplement.
I do not believe that new mathematics is generally required to make the article acceptable. The main gap is editorial selection and reorganization. There is one possible exception: if the authors insist on retaining the joint marked theorem as a headline result under the present finite-window title, they should either formulate and prove the corresponding finite-window marked theorem or explain much more directly why the one-layer formulation is the natural finite-window consequence. Otherwise it should be demoted or moved.
The single objection most likely to sink the paper is the absence of a single controlled article architecture. A referee could reasonably conclude that the paper contains too many adjacent results, repeated source disclaimers, and a second theorem suite after the main theorem has already been proved. This objection is fixable. I would invite a substantial revision rather than recommend rejection, because the exact finite-window correspondences and the completion of the nonexposed large-deviation lower bounds form a coherent and publishable JNT article once the surrounding material is disciplined.

PART ONE â€” THE HOUSE STYLE, LEARNED FROM ACTUAL RECENT PAPERS
1. What recent JNT papers actually look like
I treated â€œrecentâ€ as approximately 2021â€“2026 and compared the manuscript with a cross-section of papers published or accepted in JNT: short classical-number-theory papers, medium-length analytic and probabilistic papers, and at least one article exceeding forty pages. The relevant comparison set includes Browningâ€“Shparlinski on square-free polynomial values, Chowâ€“Jones on the Fibonacci partition function, Liâ€“Wangâ€“Wangâ€“Yi on covering systems, Granthamâ€“Granville on primes in recurrence sequences, and recent longer papers on Iwasawa modules and random characteristic polynomials. The journal accepts a broad range of authorial styles, so there is no rigid template, but there is a recognizable editorial register. arXiv+4ç§‘å­¦ç›´é€šè½¦+4arXiv+4
How a typical paper opens
A normal JNT paper opens by putting a familiar arithmetic object or problem on the page immediately. It then gives enough history to locate the precise question, formulates the new result, and moves into proofs. The opening is usually problem-driven rather than manifesto-driven.
The main theorem commonly appears on pages 2â€“4. It need not be on the first page. Browningâ€“Shparlinski first state the square-free-value problem, describe the earlier range, define the family being averaged, and then give Theorem 1.1. Chowâ€“Jones introduce the Fibonacci partition function, explain the misleading naÃ¯ve prediction, show the numerical phenomenon, and state Theorem 1.1 on the third preprint page. The covering-systems paper gives a somewhat longer history and the necessary function-field definitions before stating its main theorem near the end of the introduction. Thus JNT readily permits either â€œproblem, history, theoremâ€ or â€œproblem, example/computation, theorem,â€ but it does not normally postpone the result until after a general essay on the paperâ€™s architecture. arXiv arXiv arXiv
For an ordinary 15â€“30-page paper, the introduction is often roughly 8â€“15% of the article. It may rise toward 15â€“20% when substantial history, examples, or conjectural heuristics are essential. In a forty- or fifty-page article, an introduction of five or six pages is not itself abnormal. The deciding question is whether those pages create a hierarchy or merely inventory everything that follows.
Your introduction occupies a little over six pages before Section 2 starts, so approximately 12% of the 52-page main article. The proportion is normal for JNT. The density and function of those pages are not.
How much explanatory prose is normal
Recent JNT papers are not austere lemma warehouses. Authors commonly give:


one or two paragraphs at the beginning of a section explaining the next mathematical move;


a sentence before a proposition explaining why it is needed;


a brief observation inside a proof when a construction changes direction;


a remark after a result when there is a genuine arithmetic consequence, limitation, or comparison.


But the body remains theorem-proof dominated. As a rough reading impression rather than a measured journal statistic, perhaps two-thirds to three-quarters of a conventional JNT body consists of definitions, estimates, formal arguments, and proofs. Explanatory prose is concentrated at points of transition. It is not repeated before and after each theorem.
Chowâ€“Jones are a useful close comparator. Their introduction gives motivation and numerical evidence, but once the proof begins, the prose is local and operational: a case is introduced because it must be counted, a recurrence is motivated because the previous count produces it, and the proof proceeds. Browningâ€“Shparlinski similarly give substantial contextual prose in the introduction, then move to compact preliminaries and sustained technical work. arXiv arXiv
How proofs are written
A short proof that delegates its substance to an existing theorem is entirely acceptable in JNT when the result really is an immediate application, a standard estimate, or a change of conventions. Browningâ€“Shparlinski, for example, prove one preliminary bound by referring directly to Stewart, Lagrangeâ€™s theorem, and Henselâ€™s lemma. arXiv
But the journal expects the article to carry the argument at precisely those points where the authors claim a new translation, endpoint treatment, arithmetic normalization, or strengthening. â€œApply [X]â€ is not enough when the contribution consists in showing that [X] applies with different indexing or at a previously excluded endpoint. Conversely, once such a transfer has been verified, JNT does not reward reproducing every branch of the source theory merely to demonstrate thoroughness.
Routine verifications are normally handled in one of three ways:


a sentence inside the proof;


a short lemma when the fact will be reused materially;


an appendix only when the computation is lengthy and genuinely distracts from the principal argument.


A formally named theorem whose proof is â€œthis is exactly the preceding corollaryâ€ is not the usual register. Nor is a succession of formally named statements each memorializing one stage of the authorsâ€™ checking process.
Appendices and supplementary material
The dominant custom in the recent JNT papers I examined is to carry the mathematical article in one document. Many have no appendix at all. Browningâ€“Shparlinskiâ€™s table of contents runs directly from the introduction through preliminaries, technical sections, proofs, and references. The accepted covering-systems paper similarly has three main sections and no appended second article. Chowâ€“Jones is essentially introduction, the main counting argument, recurrence solution, references. arXiv arXiv arXiv
My practical estimate of the house custom is:


0â€“10% appended material: entirely ordinary;


10â€“20%: noticeable but acceptable when it consists of computations, data, technical uniformity lemmas, or convention-heavy checks;


about 27%, as in a 52-page main article plus a 19-page supplement: distinctly unusual.


The issue is not a formal prohibition. It is that a supplement of that size often signals one of two editorial problems: either essential proof material has been displaced from the paper, or the package contains a second paper that has not been separated.
The uploaded object contains only the 52-page main article; it ends with the references and author addresses on page 52. The supplement is described in the article as containing â€œconditional arithmetic and integer moment consequences,â€ and later as containing â€œconditional microcanonical, dyadic-ray, and integer-moment consequences outside the main theorem spine,â€ but the supplement itself is not attached. I can therefore assess the 52:19 architecture and the categories named by the authors, but not the supplementâ€™s paragraph-level style or internal organization.   
Prose register
First-person plural is normal: â€œwe prove,â€ â€œwe shall use,â€ â€œwe now apply.â€ Impersonal constructions also occur, but JNT does not expect a forced passive voice. Results are referred to by number. A section opening may remind the reader of the preceding result and state the next objective. Motivation is repeated only when the mathematical perspective genuinely changes.
The register is confident but not promotional. Authors do not usually keep an account, throughout the paper, of which sentence is imported, which result is a transfer, which claim is not being made, which adjacent manuscript does what, and which possible theorem remains open. That information belongs principally in one well-written passage in the introduction and, where necessary, in a precise local attribution.
The principal tells of a non-JNT register
The following are the common warning signs:


the introduction reads like an extended abstract plus a response to earlier referees;


every theorem is followed by a miniature proof synopsis;


elementary consequences and major results receive the same ceremonial presentation;


a paper repeatedly assures the reader that it is not claiming things;


an independent second theorem family begins late in the article;


the appendix or supplement is large enough to be another article;


transitions describe the document rather than advancing the mathematics;


the conclusion repeats the contribution inventory already given in the abstract and introduction.


Your manuscript exhibits several of these, despite having a genuinely JNT-like mathematical core.

This is the clearest point at which the paper reads as machine-assisted or referee-conditioned. It behaves as though every possible misunderstanding must be preempted in every available location. A human journal article normally trusts one precise contribution paragraph to do that work.

A workable structure would be:

Delete subsection 1.4 in its present form. Its attribution content should be condensed to one paragraph placed before the organization paragraph. Mention the companion manuscript once, in a final sentence or footnote, only insofar as necessary to delimit dependence.
Section 2: Finite-window fibres
The definitions are clear and well ordered. Establishing the bijection Vmâ€‹ before defining the fold is sensible. The single-overflow observation gives the residue model a concrete operational meaning. 
The section is nevertheless more formal than necessary. Proposition 2.2, Proposition 2.4, Remark 2.5, and Corollary 2.6 occupy almost two pages to establish a setup that can be given in roughly one page. None is objectionable alone; the aggregate gives elementary preliminaries the same visual weight as the later renewal and LDP arguments.

4. Does it read as machine-assisted?
Yes, in its editorial layer it does.
I do not mean that the mathematics reads fabricated or that the proofs lack mathematical individuality. The affine transfer, the orbit-filling construction, and the critical renewal argument have real internal shape. The machine-assisted impression comes from how the text packages and repeatedly explains them.
The strongest specific signs are these.
Repeated contribution ledgers
The paper gives essentially the same imported-versus-new accounting in:


the abstract;


the second page of the introduction;


subsection 1.4;


Remark 5.14;


the conclusion.


Compare the early distinction between transferred and finite-window information, the full contribution inventory in subsection 1.4, the source audit in Remark 5.14, and the closing inventory.    
A human author usually resolves this anxiety once and then writes the paper. Here, the prose keeps reopening the boundary as though every section must be independently safe against misreading.
Throat-clearing and structural announcements
There are many sentences of the form:


 succeeded in 175ms:

â€œThe following lemma records exactlyâ€¦â€


â€œFor clarity, eventual equality is a separate statementâ€¦â€


â€œWe now show thatâ€¦â€


â€œWe record the direct finite-layer recoveryâ€¦â€


â€œIt remains toâ€¦â€


â€œWe make the boundary passage â€¦ explicit.â€


â€œThe following pressure statement is retained becauseâ€¦â€


Some of these are useful. In aggregate they create the sense that the text is continually announcing its own procedure instead of simply performing it. The sentence that a pressure statement is â€œretained becauseâ€ its normalization is used later is especially revealing: it sounds like an editorial note left in the published narrative.   
Exhaustive enumeration where selection is needed
The introduction gives four headline theorems, their formulas, proof locations, and proof mechanisms. Subsection 1.4 then enumerates every new item and every imported item. Remark 5.14 repeats the source classification almost result by result.
The issue is not accuracy. The issue is editorial judgment. A journal article should choose which three ideas the reader must carry. This manuscript repeatedly gives the reader all of them.
Flat emphasis
Theorem 3.1, whose proof is the preceding corollary, is presented with the same theorem typography as the affine correspondence. The candidate pressure strip, later superseded by the exact pressure theorem, receives a named theorem and numerical width. A non-solution of an arithmetic interface receives a proposition plus two long remarks. Meanwhile, the genuinely decisive orbit-filling idea appears amid the same sequence of named statements.
The mathematics is uneven, as good mathematics should be. The presentation suppresses that unevenness.
Symmetrical sentence construction
The prose repeatedly uses balanced pairs:


first identity/second identity;


pointwise description/multiset description;


imported pressure/finite-window conclusion;


exposed slopes/nonexposed slopes;


one-dimensional filling/two-dimensional filling;


companion paper uses this but not that, while this paper uses that but not this.


Some of this reflects real structure. But the recurrence is strong enough that the prose acquires a templated rhythm.
Overall diagnosis
The manuscript does not read like raw machine output. It reads like a technically serious paper that has been machine-assisted through several rounds of defensive expansion and symmetry-seeking revision. The cure is not cosmetic synonym replacement. It is deletion and hierarchy:


say the contribution boundary once;


allow minor facts to remain minor;


let the central proof be much longer than its surroundings;


stop explaining why every included paragraph was included.


That would make the authorsâ€™ mathematical voice much more visible.

PART TWO â€” YOU ARE THE REFEREE
Recommendation: Major revisions
To the Editor:
The manuscript studies a finite folding map from binary Fibonacci sums to legal Zeckendorf windows. Its principal results give two exact descriptions of the fibre multiplicities, transfer these descriptions to local multiplicity spectra, identify critical finite-size laws at the freezing point of the associated pressure, and prove a full large-deviation principle by supplying lower bounds at the nonexposed slopes. A marked version yields a joint costâ€“multiplicity rate function with an affine coexistence face.
The subject is appropriate for the Journal of Number Theory. The exact affine correspondence and two-layer identity provide a clear arithmetic entry point, and the orbit-filling argument used to complete the large-deviation lower bound is sufficiently concrete that the probabilistic conclusions remain attached to the underlying Fibonacci arithmetic. The manuscript is also careful about attribution: the known golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution pressure and the established extremal classification are not presented as new.
My recommendation is nevertheless major revision rather than acceptance in the present form.
The central problem is not the amount of technical detail by itself. It is that the article has not chosen a sufficiently strict main spine. It currently reads as a combination of:


an article on exact finite-window correspondences;


an article on local and critical Fibonacci-partition thermodynamics;


an article on one-layer and marked large deviations;


a prospectus for conditional prime-support and active-cutoff questions;


a substantial separate supplement.


The first three topics are mathematically connected, but the manuscript presents each as a nearly autonomous theorem suite. This gives subordinate, transferred, intermediate, and principal results comparable textual weight.
The introduction illustrates the problem. The main results are stated early, which is welcome, but each is accompanied by a proof synopsis and location notice. A later subsection then gives a full contribution boundary, a companion-paper disclaimer, and a section-by-section map. Closely related source and contribution inventories recur in Remark 5.14 and the conclusion.   
Several sections retain material that appears to document the development of the project rather than the final proof architecture. Theorem 5.5 confines the pressure boundary to a numerical strip, but Proposition 5.9 subsequently determines the boundary exactly. Proposition 5.12 formulates a finite-prime-support interface, while the following remark explains in considerable detail why the desired active-cutoff theorem is not proved. These results may be useful elsewhere, but they interrupt the route from the exact finite model to the critical law and full LDP.  
The most serious structural issue is Section 6. After the finite-window LDP and critical law have been proved, the manuscript restates and substantially re-proves analogous results intrinsically for one Fibonacci layer, and then proves a joint marked LDP. The section occupies approximately seven pages and reads as a second paper rather than a short application. Moreover, the joint one-layer theorem is advertised as one of the four principal results despite the finite-window title.  
I would ask the authors to reorganize the article around the following sequence:


exact affine and interval correspondences;


local stabilization and the weighted renewal identity;


pressure normalization at the freezing corner;


critical finite-size law;


orbit-filling proof of the full finite-window LDP.


The transferred extremal classification should be stated but its full convention audit can be placed in an appendix. The long reconstruction of the Weinstein branch formulas should be shortened in the article while retaining a complete proof of the endpoint improvement actually needed. The intermediate transition-strip theorem and compact-operator remark should be deleted or moved. The finite-prime-support interface should be placed in the supplement. Section 6 should be reduced to concise corollaries, or separated from the article.
The prose also requires a substantial editorial pass. The manuscript repeatedly uses contribution disclaimers, structure announcements, and statements that explain why another statement is being retained. The result is unusually defensive and gives an impression of machine-assisted uniformity. The authors should state the contribution boundary once in the introduction, retain exact local citations, and remove the repeated audits from the abstract, Remark 5.14, and conclusion.
The stated 52-page article with a 19-page supplement is also outside the usual balance for this journal. I have been supplied only the main article, so I cannot assess the supplement internally. On the description in the main text, however, the conditional arithmetic and integer-moment consequences appear nonessential to the main theorem chain. They should remain separate, and if they constitute a substantial coherent article they should not be presented as a nineteen-page supplement.
I do not believe that new mathematics is generally required to make the article acceptable. The main gap is editorial selection and reorganization. There is one possible exception: if the authors insist on retaining the joint marked theorem as a headline result under the present finite-window title, they should either formulate and prove the corresponding finite-window marked theorem or explain much more directly why the one-layer formulation is the natural finite-window consequence. Otherwise it should be demoted or moved.
The single objection most likely to sink the paper is the absence of a single controlled article architecture. A referee could reasonably conclude that the paper contains too many adjacent results, repeated source disclaimers, and a second theorem suite after the main theorem has already been proved. This objection is fixable. I would invite a substantial revision rather than recommend rejection, because the exact finite-window correspondences and the completion of the nonexposed large-deviation lower bounds form a coherent and publishable JNT article once the surrounding material is disciplined.

name: writing-plans
description: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans â€” one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** â€” never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code â€” the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step â€” if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself â€” not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags â€” any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review â€” just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

===== artifacts\bernoulli_convolution_priority_audit.md =====
# Golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution priority audit

Checked 2026-08-15 against primary papers or journal metadata.  This audit
uses the convention
\[
\tau_\mu(q)=\lim_{n\to\infty}
 \frac{\log\sum_{I\in\mathcal N_n}\mu(I)^q}{\log(\varphi^{-n})}.
\]

## Direct finite-count identification

- N. Sidorov and A. Vershik, *Ergodic properties of the Erdos measure, the
  entropy of the goldenshift, and related problems*, Monatsh. Math. 126
  (1998), 215-261, DOI 10.1007/BF01367764; preprint arXiv:math/9612223.
  Section 2 identifies \(f_n(k)\) both as the number of finite Fibonacci
  representations and as the vertex frequency on level \(n\) of the Fibonacci
  graph, and states that \(2^{-n}f_n(k)\) gives the finite masses converging to
  the Erdos measure.  Thus these are the manuscript's representation
  coefficients up to its unit/index convention, not an analogous object.

## Local dimensions and positive-q spectrum

- T.-Y. Hu, *The local dimensions of the Bernoulli convolution associated
  with the golden number*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 349 (1997), 2917-2940,
  DOI 10.1090/S0002-9947-97-01474-8.  This predates the manuscript's
  normalized log-multiplicity discussion and determines extremal local
  dimensions for the same golden-ratio convolution.
- K.-S. Lau and S.-M. Ngai, *L^q-spectrum of the Bernoulli convolution
  associated with the golden ratio*, Studia Math. 131 (1998), 225-251.
  The paper's main result gives an exact formula for the golden-ratio
  \(L^q\)-spectrum for every \(q>0\).  Its block denominator
  \(Q_J=[1\ 1]P_J(1,1)^T\), block length \(2k+3\), and normalized mass
  \(2^{-(2k+3)}Q_J\) match, respectively, the renewal-letter denominator,
  letter cost, and normalized Fibonacci representation mass used here.

## All-real spectrum and negative phase transition

- D.-J. Feng and E. Olivier, *Multifractal analysis of weak Gibbs measures
  and phase transition: application to some Bernoulli convolutions*, Ergodic
  Theory Dynam. Systems 23 (2003), 1751-1784,
  DOI 10.1017/S0143385703000051.  Theorem 2.9 proves that the Erdos measure is
  weak Gibbs.  Theorem 2.10 gives its complete \(L^q\)-spectrum and a critical
  \(q_c<0\) such that the spectrum is linear exactly for \(q\le q_c\).
  Appendix Theorem A.1 proves nondifferentiability at the critical value.
  The paper explicitly calls this a first-order phase transition.
- D.-J. Feng, *The limited Rademacher functions and Bernoulli convolutions
  associated with Pisot numbers*, Adv. Math. 195 (2005), 24-101,
  DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2004.06.011.  Theorem 1.3(i), proved through the
  golden-ratio calculation in Theorem 4.4, gives the \(L^q\)-spectrum for
  every real \(q\).  It defines \(x(q)\) by the same matrix-block renewal
  series, proves a unique \(q_0<-2\), gives the positive-root branch for
  \(q>q_0\), sets \(x(q)=1\) for \(q\le q_0\), and proves that \(x\) is not
  differentiable at \(q_0\).  Feng's author bibliography records 1999
  preprints containing the underlying Parts I-II; the citable final article
  is 2005.

## Exact normalization and coverage

At level \(m\), a net-interval mass is \(2^{-m}f_m(k)\), while the geometric
scale is \(\varphi^{-m}\).  Therefore
\[
\log\sum_I\mu(I)^t=-mt\log2+\log\sum_k f_m(k)^t
\]
and hence, after the manuscript's finite layer/window index changes,
\[
P(t)=t\log2-\tau_\mu(t)\log\varphi.
\]
Consequently the prior literature covers: existence for every real tilt; the
positive implicit pressure equation; the negative linear/frozen phase; the
negative critical value as the solution of the block-renewal equation; its
first-order nondifferentiability; and the generic Legendre multifractal
formalism.  These cannot be novelty claims of the manuscript.

The present renewal alphabet sums over all reduced \(p/q\in(0,1)\).  At the
critical boundary its letter sum is
\[
\sum_{q\ge2}\varphi_{\rm E}(q)q^{-s}
=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)}-1.
\]
Thus Feng's implicit condition becomes
\(\zeta(\sigma_0-1)/\zeta(\sigma_0)=2\).  The located papers do not state this
totient/zeta evaluation, the critical constants \(2/\mu_C\) and \(4/\mu_C\),
the uniform finite-layer coexistence limit, the explicit orbit-filling lower
bound at nonexposed uniform-layer slopes, or the finite-window affine/fiber
identities.  Those are the defensible incremental claims, subject to the
proofs in the manuscript; absence from these sources is not a claim that no
other paper contains them.

Verdict: split
The revision was worth making because it removes a credibility problem: the introduction now tells the reader exactly which results are independent and exactly where the scalar denominator-layer asymptotic enters. But that clarification does not make the two narratives inseparable. It confirms that the genuine common spine is the scalar asymptotic, the critical generator-cost tail, and its renewal transfer; the total-variation theorem and most of the finite-window thermodynamics remain logically autonomous. 
My definite valuation is:

The total-variation theorem itself gives the joint context law, defect, location, side lengths, and denominator factorization, rather than merely a partition-sum estimate. The fact that the downstream application uses the scalar corollary rather than the full total-variation conclusion is not a coherence defect in Paper A. A paper may prove a stronger structural theorem and then use one sharp corollary in an application. The problem in the 73-page version is not that logical fact; it is that another 40-plus pages develop a largely autonomous second theory around it.
Paper A would therefore have:


substantially higher significance density;


a single visible arithmetic-probabilistic mechanism;


no competition between the Brocot theorem and recovered pressure results;


a correction that functions as part of a proof mechanism rather than as a separate priority headline;


a natural reason to include the Fibonacci material.


I would not call it a certain TAMS paper. The remaining rejection route is significance: a referee could still decide that the total-variation theorem is a specialized sharpening of a known scalar asymptotic and that the stable-renewal application, though exact, is too narrow. But after the split, that becomes a genuinely contestable judgment rather than an almost automatic coherence objection.

It has classical number-theoretic objects, an exact correction to an existing continued-fraction calculation, a structural probability theorem, explicit zeta constants, and a new critical-renewal consequence. Its likely JNT failure modes would be a serious priority collision or a problem with the correction, not scope or architecture.
Thus the rational submission sequence for Paper A is TAMS first, JNT as a strong fallback.

Respectable specialist venue: 80â€“90%

This is not a collection of appendices that survives only because Theorem A is nearby.
The important qualification is editorial rather than mathematical: Paper B must stop presenting every recovered pressure statement, transferred extremal result, and auxiliary interface at equal visual weight. Its publishable core is narrower than its present theorem count, but the core is real.

I would split.
I would submit Paper A to TAMS. I would prepare Paper B separately for JNT, with its introduction centered on the exact finite-window correspondence and the completion of the LDP across the freezing corner.
I would not submit the present combined article directly to JNT merely because that is the predicted median outcome. That is the safer one-paper decision, but it gives away the principal option value:


Paper A becomes more likely than not to pass TAMS after the split;


it has a strong JNT fallback;


Paper B remains independently publishable and has a real JNT chance;


the split is intellectually natural rather than artificial, because the manuscript itself now states the logical autonomy of the two sides.


The asymmetric-dependency revision has therefore done more than improve the introduction. It has supplied the authors with the correct cut line.
My author decision would be: two papers, Paper A to TAMS first, Paper B to JNT.

===== README.md =====
# Finite-Window Zeckendorf Thermodynamics

This directory contains the main article and its separately compiled
supplement. The primary submission target is the *Journal of Number Theory*.

The article studies exact finite-window Fibonacci coefficient spectra. Its
main results are the affine coefficient-spectrum correspondence, the
pointwise partition-difference formula, the exact two-layer identity, local
spectral stabilization, critical finite-window Gibbs and coexistence laws,
the completion of the large-deviation principle across the freezing corner,
and the joint cost--multiplicity large-deviation principle. Pressure formulas
from the golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution literature and the transferred
extremal classification are used as subordinate inputs, with their provenance
stated in the manuscript.

The companion article, *Brocot Condensation and Critical Fibonacci Renewal*,
contains the total-variation condensation law, the corrected scalar
denominator-layer asymptotic, and the arithmetic critical renewal
consequences.

## Build

The bibliography is written directly in `sec_references.tex`; BibTeX is not
used. Build the main article before the supplement so `xr-hyper` can resolve
cross-document references:

```powershell
latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error main.tex
latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error supplement.tex
```

The expected outputs are `main.pdf` and `supplement.pdf`. Reproduction commands
for the computational checks are in `artifacts/REPRODUCE.md`.

\begin{abstract}
We study the multiplicity spectrum of the finite map obtained by folding
binary Fibonacci sums into the legal Zeckendorf window.  The fibers admit
two exact descriptions.  An affine residue permutation identifies them
pointwise with a finite Fibonacci coefficient spectrum and yields a
partition-difference formula; an interval identity identifies their complete
multiset with the classical Fibonacci partition function on two consecutive
layers.  These identities transfer the known extremal classification while
also giving exact local spectral stabilization.

The exponential pressure is the published \(L^q\)-spectrum of the
golden-ratio Bernoulli convolution in an affine normalization and is used as
an input, not claimed as an independent contribution.  At its freezing
corner we prove finite-window critical Gibbs and coexistence laws.  The
corner leaves a whole interval of slopes outside the black-box lower bound
of the G\"artner--Ellis theorem.  An injective generator-orbit filling
construction supplies every missing slope and completes the full large
deviation principle.  Retaining generator cost gives a joint
cost--multiplicity large deviation principle whose coexistence region is an
affine face of the rate surface.
\end{abstract}

===== artifacts\bernoulli_convolution_priority_audit.md =====
# Golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution priority audit

Checked 2026-08-15 against primary papers or journal metadata.  This audit
uses the convention
\[
\tau_\mu(q)=\lim_{n\to\infty}
 \frac{\log\sum_{I\in\mathcal N_n}\mu(I)^q}{\log(\varphi^{-n})}.
\]

## Direct finite-count identification

- N. Sidorov and A. Vershik, *Ergodic properties of the Erdos measure, the
  entropy of the goldenshift, and related problems*, Monatsh. Math. 126
  (1998), 215-261, DOI 10.1007/BF01367764; preprint arXiv:math/9612223.
  Section 2 identifies \(f_n(k)\) both as the number of finite Fibonacci
  representations and as the vertex frequency on level \(n\) of the Fibonacci
  graph, and states that \(2^{-n}f_n(k)\) gives the finite masses converging to
  the Erdos measure.  Thus these are the manuscript's representation
  coefficients up to its unit/index convention, not an analogous object.

## Local dimensions and positive-q spectrum

- T.-Y. Hu, *The local dimensions of the Bernoulli convolution associated
  with the golden number*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 349 (1997), 2917-2940,
  DOI 10.1090/S0002-9947-97-01474-8.  This predates the manuscript's
  normalized log-multiplicity discussion and determines extremal local
  dimensions for the same golden-ratio convolution.
- K.-S. Lau and S.-M. Ngai, *L^q-spectrum of the Bernoulli convolution
  associated with the golden ratio*, Studia Math. 131 (1998), 225-251.
  The paper's main result gives an exact formula for the golden-ratio
  \(L^q\)-spectrum for every \(q>0\).  Its block denominator
  \(Q_J=[1\ 1]P_J(1,1)^T\), block length \(2k+3\), and normalized mass
  \(2^{-(2k+3)}Q_J\) match, respectively, the renewal-letter denominator,
  letter cost, and normalized Fibonacci representation mass used here.

## All-real spectrum and negative phase transition

- D.-J. Feng and E. Olivier, *Multifractal analysis of weak Gibbs measures
  and phase transition: application to some Bernoulli convolutions*, Ergodic
  Theory Dynam. Systems 23 (2003), 1751-1784,
  DOI 10.1017/S0143385703000051.  Theorem 2.9 proves that the Erdos measure is
  weak Gibbs.  Theorem 2.10 gives its complete \(L^q\)-spectrum and a critical
  \(q_c<0\) such that the spectrum is linear exactly for \(q\le q_c\).
  Appendix Theorem A.1 proves nondifferentiability at the critical value.
  The paper explicitly calls this a first-order phase transition.
- D.-J. Feng, *The limited Rademacher functions and Bernoulli convolutions
  associated with Pisot numbers*, Adv. Math. 195 (2005), 24-101,
  DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2004.06.011.  Theorem 1.3(i), proved through the
  golden-ratio calculation in Theorem 4.4, gives the \(L^q\)-spectrum for
  every real \(q\).  It defines \(x(q)\) by the same matrix-block renewal
  series, proves a unique \(q_0<-2\), gives the positive-root branch for
  \(q>q_0\), sets \(x(q)=1\) for \(q\le q_0\), and proves that \(x\) is not
  differentiable at \(q_0\).  Feng's author bibliography records 1999
  preprints containing the underlying Parts I-II; the citable final article
  is 2005.

## Exact normalization and coverage

At level \(m\), a net-interval mass is \(2^{-m}f_m(k)\), while the geometric
scale is \(\varphi^{-m}\).  Therefore
\[
\log\sum_I\mu(I)^t=-mt\log2+\log\sum_k f_m(k)^t
\]
and hence, after the manuscript's finite layer/window index changes,
\[
P(t)=t\log2-\tau_\mu(t)\log\varphi.
\]
Consequently the prior literature covers: existence for every real tilt; the
positive implicit pressure equation; the negative linear/frozen phase; the
negative critical value as the solution of the block-renewal equation; its
first-order nondifferentiability; and the generic Legendre multifractal
formalism.  These cannot be novelty claims of the manuscript.

The present renewal alphabet sums over all reduced \(p/q\in(0,1)\).  At the
critical boundary its letter sum is
\[
\sum_{q\ge2}\varphi_{\rm E}(q)q^{-s}
=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)}-1.
\]
Thus Feng's implicit condition becomes
\(\zeta(\sigma_0-1)/\zeta(\sigma_0)=2\).  The located papers do not state this
totient/zeta evaluation, the critical constants \(2/\mu_C\) and \(4/\mu_C\),
the uniform finite-layer coexistence limit, the explicit orbit-filling lower
bound at nonexposed uniform-layer slopes, or the finite-window affine/fiber
identities.  Those are the defensible incremental claims, subject to the
proofs in the manuscript; absence from these sources is not a claim that no
other paper contains them.

Verdict: split
The revision was worth making because it removes a credibility problem: the introduction now tells the reader exactly which results are independent and exactly where the scalar denominator-layer asymptotic enters. But that clarification does not make the two narratives inseparable. It confirms that the genuine common spine is the scalar asymptotic, the critical generator-cost tail, and its renewal transfer; the total-variation theorem and most of the finite-window thermodynamics remain logically autonomous. 
My definite valuation is:

The scalar consequence then corrects the leading coefficient of the pre-existing local sum while disclaiming the remaining coefficients.  At the critical point, that arithmetic result supplies the tail constant, the renewal correction of order m3âˆ’Ïƒ0â€‹, and the stable domain of attraction.  
The fact that the downstream application uses the scalar corollary rather than the full total-variation conclusion is not a coherence defect in Paper A. A paper may prove a stronger structural theorem and then use one sharp corollary in an application. The problem in the 73-page version is not that logical fact; it is that another 40-plus pages develop a largely autonomous second theory around it.
Paper A would therefore have:


substantially higher significance density;


a single visible arithmetic-probabilistic mechanism;


no competition between the Brocot theorem and recovered pressure results;


a correction that functions as part of a proof mechanism rather than as a separate priority headline;


a natural reason to include the Fibonacci material.


I would not call it a certain TAMS paper. The remaining rejection route is significance: a referee could still decide that the total-variation theorem is a specialized sharpening of a known scalar asymptotic and that the stable-renewal application, though exact, is too narrow. But after the split, that becomes a genuinely contestable judgment rather than an almost automatic coherence objection.
JNT: 82â€“90%, central estimate 86%

It has classical number-theoretic objects, an exact correction to an existing continued-fraction calculation, a structural probability theorem, explicit zeta constants, and a new critical-renewal consequence. Its likely JNT failure modes would be a serious priority collision or a problem with the correction, not scope or architecture.
Thus the rational submission sequence for Paper A is TAMS first, JNT as a strong fallback.

JNT: 50â€“65%
JNT is realistic but not automatic. Paper B would have to be rebuilt around the exact finite-window correspondence and the nonexposed-slope LDPâ€”not around the recovered pressure or the transferred maximum formulas.
I would put its median outcome slightly below the median outcome of the present combined article, because it loses the Brocot theorem as its strongest externally recognizable result. But it remains a credible JNT submission.
Respectable specialist venue: 80â€“90%
Splitting does not cost the authors a publishable paper. It relocates Paper B.
Even if JNT declined it on significance or density grounds, the exact correspondences, local spectral results, and completed LDP are enough for a respectable specialist venue in number theory, numeration, arithmetic dynamics, or probabilistic combinatorics. This is not a collection of appendices that survives only because Theorem A is nearby.
The important qualification is editorial rather than mathematical: Paper B must stop presenting every recovered pressure statement, transferred extremal result, and auxiliary interface at equal visual weight. Its publishable core is narrower than its present theorem count, but the core is real.
3. The third option: a spine-only main article plus supplement
There is one viable third architecture:
Keep in the main article


the present Section 2 in substance;


a compressed definition of the classical Fibonacci partition function and Weinstein generator coordinates;


the weighted generator renewal identity, preferably in a one-layer form first;


the exact critical denominator-layer tail and constant;


the stable law;


the m3âˆ’Ïƒ0â€‹ correction;


at most a short finite-window corollary obtained from the two-layer identity.


Move out of the main article
The following current material should move as a single defined block:


essentially all of current Sections 3 and 4: the residue fold, Fourier formula, affine subset-sum transfer, and partition-difference correspondence;


Section 5.1: the full extremal transfer, maximizing-residue tables, and recurrence;


Proposition 5.5 and the recovered frozen-pressure discussion;


Theorems 6.1â€“6.5: local spectrum, unnormalized limits, Gibbs pole, Tauberian orbit law, and transition-strip bounds;


Lemmas 6.7â€“6.8 and Proposition 6.9: Knauf normalization and pressure recovery;


Theorem 6.10: the full finite-window LDP;


Proposition 6.12 and the active-cutoff interface;


Theorems 7.1 and 7.2: the full one-layer and joint large-deviation packages.


The main article would then be approximately 37â€“42 pages, with a 28â€“34-page supplement.
That would raise the TAMS probability to roughly 45â€“55%. It would improve the first-read density and make the main theorem spine obvious. But I do not recommend it.
First, the supplement would contain almost a complete second paper. Reviewers would still see that fact, and some would simply request a split. Second, the manuscript already has a separately compiled supplement for conditional arithmetic, dyadic, and integer-moment consequences; adding another large autonomous block would produce an awkward main-paper-plus-two-shadow-papers package.   Third, this option destroys most of Paper Bâ€™s publication value while gaining less TAMS probability than an actual split.
A modest supplement moveâ€”only Fourier details, extremal tables, pressure-recovery proofs, and the prime-support interfaceâ€”would save perhaps 12â€“16 pages, but it would not cure the two-narrative problem. The article would remain a Brocot paper followed by a large autonomous Fibonacci thermodynamics paper.
So the third option exists, but it is dominated by splitting.
4. What I would do as an author
I would split.
I would submit Paper A to TAMS. I would prepare Paper B separately for JNT, with its introduction centered on the exact finite-window correspondence and the completion of the LDP across the freezing corner.
I would not submit the present combined article directly to JNT merely because that is the predicted median outcome. That is the safer one-paper decision, but it gives away the principal option value:


Paper A becomes more likely than not to pass TAMS after the split;


it has a strong JNT fallback;


Paper B remains independently publishable and has a real JNT chance;


the split is intellectually natural rather than artificial, because the manuscript itself now states the logical autonomy of the two sides.


The asymmetric-dependency revision has therefore done more than improve the introduction. It has supplied the authors with the correct cut line.
My author decision would be: two papers, Paper A to TAMS first, Paper B to JNT.

reports use Unix LF. Archived path fields contain file names rather than
checkout-specific absolute paths, and no archived file contains clock or date
fields.

## Checksum verification

Paths in `SHA256SUMS` are relative to the `artifacts` directory. From the paper
directory, run exactly:

```sh
cd artifacts && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
```

A successful check prints exactly 15 `OK` lines and no failures. The
project-local `.gitattributes` pins every file covered by the manifest to LF.

===== README.md =====
# Finite-Window Zeckendorf Thermodynamics

This directory contains the main article and its separately compiled
supplement. The primary submission target is the *Journal of Number Theory*.

The article studies exact finite-window Fibonacci coefficient spectra. Its
main results are the affine coefficient-spectrum correspondence, the
pointwise partition-difference formula, the exact two-layer identity, local
spectral stabilization, critical finite-window Gibbs and coexistence laws,
the completion of the large-deviation principle across the freezing corner,
and the joint cost--multiplicity large-deviation principle. Pressure formulas
from the golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution literature and the transferred
extremal classification are used as subordinate inputs, with their provenance
stated in the manuscript.

The companion article, *Brocot Condensation and Critical Fibonacci Renewal*,
contains the total-variation condensation law, the corrected scalar
denominator-layer asymptotic, and the arithmetic critical renewal
consequences.

## Build

The bibliography is written directly in `sec_references.tex`; BibTeX is not
used. Build the main article before the supplement so `xr-hyper` can resolve
cross-document references:

```powershell
latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error main.tex
latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error supplement.tex
```

The expected outputs are `main.pdf` and `supplement.pdf`. Reproduction commands
for the computational checks are in `artifacts/REPRODUCE.md`.

\begin{abstract}
We study the multiplicity spectrum of the finite map obtained by folding
binary Fibonacci sums into the legal Zeckendorf window.  The fibers admit
two exact descriptions.  An affine residue permutation identifies them
pointwise with a finite Fibonacci coefficient spectrum and yields a
partition-difference formula; an interval identity identifies their complete
multiset with the classical Fibonacci partition function on two consecutive
layers.  These identities transfer the known extremal classification while
also giving exact local spectral stabilization.

The exponential pressure is the published \(L^q\)-spectrum of the
golden-ratio Bernoulli convolution in an affine normalization and is used as
an input, not claimed as an independent contribution.  At its freezing
corner we prove finite-window critical Gibbs and coexistence laws.  The
corner leaves a whole interval of slopes outside the black-box lower bound
of the G\"artner--Ellis theorem.  An injective generator-orbit filling
construction supplies every missing slope and completes the full large
deviation principle.  Retaining generator cost gives a joint
cost--multiplicity large deviation principle whose coexistence region is an
affine face of the rate surface.
\end{abstract}

===== artifacts\bernoulli_convolution_priority_audit.md =====
# Golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution priority audit

Checked 2026-08-15 against primary papers or journal metadata.  This audit
uses the convention
\[
\tau_\mu(q)=\lim_{n\to\infty}
 \frac{\log\sum_{I\in\mathcal N_n}\mu(I)^q}{\log(\varphi^{-n})}.
\]

## Direct finite-count identification

- N. Sidorov and A. Vershik, *Ergodic properties of the Erdos measure, the
  entropy of the goldenshift, and related problems*, Monatsh. Math. 126
  (1998), 215-261, DOI 10.1007/BF01367764; preprint arXiv:math/9612223.
  Section 2 identifies \(f_n(k)\) both as the number of finite Fibonacci
  representations and as the vertex frequency on level \(n\) of the Fibonacci
  graph, and states that \(2^{-n}f_n(k)\) gives the finite masses converging to
  the Erdos measure.  Thus these are the manuscript's representation
  coefficients up to its unit/index convention, not an analogous object.

## Local dimensions and positive-q spectrum

- T.-Y. Hu, *The local dimensions of the Bernoulli convolution associated
  with the golden number*, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 349 (1997), 2917-2940,
  DOI 10.1090/S0002-9947-97-01474-8.  This predates the manuscript's
  normalized log-multiplicity discussion and determines extremal local
  dimensions for the same golden-ratio convolution.
- K.-S. Lau and S.-M. Ngai, *L^q-spectrum of the Bernoulli convolution
  associated with the golden ratio*, Studia Math. 131 (1998), 225-251.
  The paper's main result gives an exact formula for the golden-ratio
  \(L^q\)-spectrum for every \(q>0\).  Its block denominator
  \(Q_J=[1\ 1]P_J(1,1)^T\), block length \(2k+3\), and normalized mass
  \(2^{-(2k+3)}Q_J\) match, respectively, the renewal-letter denominator,
  letter cost, and normalized Fibonacci representation mass used here.

## All-real spectrum and negative phase transition

- D.-J. Feng and E. Olivier, *Multifractal analysis of weak Gibbs measures
  and phase transition: application to some Bernoulli convolutions*, Ergodic
  Theory Dynam. Systems 23 (2003), 1751-1784,
  DOI 10.1017/S0143385703000051.  Theorem 2.9 proves that the Erdos measure is
  weak Gibbs.  Theorem 2.10 gives its complete \(L^q\)-spectrum and a critical
  \(q_c<0\) such that the spectrum is linear exactly for \(q\le q_c\).
  Appendix Theorem A.1 proves nondifferentiability at the critical value.
  The paper explicitly calls this a first-order phase transition.
- D.-J. Feng, *The limited Rademacher functions and Bernoulli convolutions
  associated with Pisot numbers*, Adv. Math. 195 (2005), 24-101,
  DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2004.06.011.  Theorem 1.3(i), proved through the
  golden-ratio calculation in Theorem 4.4, gives the \(L^q\)-spectrum for
  every real \(q\).  It defines \(x(q)\) by the same matrix-block renewal
  series, proves a unique \(q_0<-2\), gives the positive-root branch for
  \(q>q_0\), sets \(x(q)=1\) for \(q\le q_0\), and proves that \(x\) is not
  differentiable at \(q_0\).  Feng's author bibliography records 1999
  preprints containing the underlying Parts I-II; the citable final article
  is 2005.

## Exact normalization and coverage

At level \(m\), a net-interval mass is \(2^{-m}f_m(k)\), while the geometric
scale is \(\varphi^{-m}\).  Therefore
\[
\log\sum_I\mu(I)^t=-mt\log2+\log\sum_k f_m(k)^t
\]
and hence, after the manuscript's finite layer/window index changes,
\[
P(t)=t\log2-\tau_\mu(t)\log\varphi.
\]
Consequently the prior literature covers: existence for every real tilt; the
positive implicit pressure equation; the negative linear/frozen phase; the
negative critical value as the solution of the block-renewal equation; its
first-order nondifferentiability; and the generic Legendre multifractal
formalism.  These cannot be novelty claims of the manuscript.

The present renewal alphabet sums over all reduced \(p/q\in(0,1)\).  At the
critical boundary its letter sum is
\[
\sum_{q\ge2}\varphi_{\rm E}(q)q^{-s}
=\frac{\zeta(s-1)}{\zeta(s)}-1.
\]
Thus Feng's implicit condition becomes
\(\zeta(\sigma_0-1)/\zeta(\sigma_0)=2\).  The located papers do not state this
totient/zeta evaluation, the critical constants \(2/\mu_C\) and \(4/\mu_C\),
the uniform finite-layer coexistence limit, the explicit orbit-filling lower
bound at nonexposed uniform-layer slopes, or the finite-window affine/fiber
identities.  Those are the defensible incremental claims, subject to the
proofs in the manuscript; absence from these sources is not a claim that no
other paper contains them.
