Respectable specialist venue: 80â€“90%
Splitting does not cost the authors a publishable paper. It relocates Paper B.
Even if JNT declined it on significance or density grounds, the exact correspondences, local spectral results, and completed LDP are enough for a respectable specialist venue in number theory, numeration, arithmetic dynamics, or probabilistic combinatorics. This is not a collection of appendices that survives only because Theorem A is nearby.
The important qualification is editorial rather than mathematical: Paper B must stop presenting every recovered pressure statement, transferred extremal result, and auxiliary interface at equal visual weight. Its publishable core is narrower than its present theorem count, but the core is real.
3. The third option: a spine-only main article plus supplement
There is one viable third architecture:
Keep in the main article


the present Section 2 in substance;


a compressed definition of the classical Fibonacci partition function and Weinstein generator coordinates;


the weighted generator renewal identity, preferably in a one-layer form first;


the exact critical denominator-layer tail and constant;


the stable law;


the m3âˆ’Ïƒ0â€‹ correction;


at most a short finite-window corollary obtained from the two-layer identity.


Move out of the main article
The following current material should move as a single defined block:


essentially all of current Sections 3 and 4: the residue fold, Fourier formula, affine subset-sum transfer, and partition-difference correspondence;


Section 5.1: the full extremal transfer, maximizing-residue tables, and recurrence;


Proposition 5.5 and the recovered frozen-pressure discussion;


Theorems 6.1â€“6.5: local spectrum, unnormalized limits, Gibbs pole, Tauberian orbit law, and transition-strip bounds;


Lemmas 6.7â€“6.8 and Proposition 6.9: Knauf normalization and pressure recovery;


Theorem 6.10: the full finite-window LDP;


Proposition 6.12 and the active-cutoff interface;


Theorems 7.1 and 7.2: the full one-layer and joint large-deviation packages.


The main article would then be approximately 37â€“42 pages, with a 28â€“34-page supplement.
That would raise the TAMS probability to roughly 45â€“55%. It would improve the first-read density and make the main theorem spine obvious. But I do not recommend it.
First, the supplement would contain almost a complete second paper. Reviewers would still see that fact, and some would simply request a split. Second, the manuscript already has a separately compiled supplement for conditional arithmetic, dyadic, and integer-moment consequences; adding another large autonomous block would produce an awkward main-paper-plus-two-shadow-papers package.   Third, this option destroys most of Paper Bâ€™s publication value while gaining less TAMS probability than an actual split.
A modest supplement moveâ€”only Fourier details, extremal tables, pressure-recovery proofs, and the prime-support interfaceâ€”would save perhaps 12â€“16 pages, but it would not cure the two-narrative problem. The article would remain a Brocot paper followed by a large autonomous Fibonacci thermodynamics paper.
So the third option exists, but it is dominated by splitting.
4. What I would do as an author
I would split.
I would submit Paper A to TAMS. I would prepare Paper B separately for JNT, with its introduction centered on the exact finite-window correspondence and the completion of the LDP across the freezing corner.
I would not submit the present combined article directly to JNT merely because that is the predicted median outcome. That is the safer one-paper decision, but it gives away the principal option value:


Paper A becomes more likely than not to pass TAMS after the split;


it has a strong JNT fallback;


Paper B remains independently publishable and has a real JNT chance;


the split is intellectually natural rather than artificial, because the manuscript itself now states the logical autonomy of the two sides.


The asymmetric-dependency revision has therefore done more than improve the introduction. It has supplied the authors with the correct cut line.
My author decision would be: two papers, Paper A to TAMS first, Paper B to JNT.

# Reproducing the finite-window checks

Run all commands from the paper directory. The stored run used Python 3.10.11,
NumPy 1.26.4, mpmath 1.3.0, Numba 0.64.0, and pytest. Install the dependencies
with:

```sh
python -m pip install "numpy==1.26.4" "mpmath==1.3.0" "numba==0.64.0" pytest
```

## Verification commands

```sh
python -m pytest artifacts -q
python artifacts/verify_deepening_delta.py --output artifacts/deepening_delta_verification.txt
python artifacts/verify_real_tilt_pressure.py
python artifacts/verify_speed_separation.py --output artifacts/speed_separation_verification.txt
```

```text
RESULT: 0 failures / 0 counterexamples
RESULT: 0 numerical failures / full-LDP orbit-padding audit passed
STATUS: PASS
```

The first two verifiers also regenerate `ldp_rate_shape.csv`,
`real_tilt_pressure.csv`, and `real_tilt_rate.csv`. The CSV records and text
reports use Unix LF. Archived path fields contain file names rather than
checkout-specific absolute paths, and no archived file contains clock or date
fields.

## Checksum verification

Paths in `SHA256SUMS` are relative to the `artifacts` directory. From the paper
directory, run exactly:

```sh
cd artifacts && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
```

A successful check prints exactly 15 `OK` lines and no failures. The
project-local `.gitattributes` pins every file covered by the manifest to LF.

===== README.md =====
# Finite-Window Zeckendorf Thermodynamics

This directory contains the main article and its separately compiled
supplement. The primary submission target is the *Journal of Number Theory*.

The article studies exact finite-window Fibonacci coefficient spectra. Its
main results are the affine coefficient-spectrum correspondence, the
pointwise partition-difference formula, the exact two-layer identity, local
spectral stabilization, critical finite-window Gibbs and coexistence laws,
the completion of the large-deviation principle across the freezing corner,
and the joint cost--multiplicity large-deviation principle. Pressure formulas
from the golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution literature and the transferred
extremal classification are used as subordinate inputs, with their provenance
stated in the manuscript.

The companion article, *Brocot Condensation and Critical Fibonacci Renewal*,
contains the total-variation condensation law, the corrected scalar
denominator-layer asymptotic, and the arithmetic critical renewal
consequences.

## Build

The bibliography is written directly in `sec_references.tex`; BibTeX is not
used. Build the main article before the supplement so `xr-hyper` can resolve
cross-document references:

```powershell
latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error main.tex
latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error supplement.tex
```

The expected outputs are `main.pdf` and `supplement.pdf`. Reproduction commands
for the computational checks are in `artifacts/REPRODUCE.md`.

\begin{abstract}
We study the multiplicity spectrum of the finite map obtained by folding
binary Fibonacci sums into the legal Zeckendorf window.  The fibers admit
two exact descriptions.  An affine residue permutation identifies them
pointwise with a finite Fibonacci coefficient spectrum and yields a
partition-difference formula; an interval identity identifies their complete
multiset with the classical Fibonacci partition function on two consecutive
layers.  These identities transfer the known extremal classification while
also giving exact local spectral stabilization.

The exponential pressure is the published \(L^q\)-spectrum of the
golden-ratio Bernoulli convolution in an affine normalization and is used as
an input, not claimed as an independent contribution.  At its freezing
corner we prove finite-window critical Gibbs and coexistence laws.  The
corner leaves a whole interval of slopes outside the black-box lower bound
of the G\"artner--Ellis theorem.  An injective generator-orbit filling
construction supplies every missing slope and completes the full large
deviation principle.  Retaining generator cost gives a joint
cost--multiplicity large deviation principle whose coexistence region is an
affine face of the rate surface.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Let \(F_0=0,F_1=F_2=1\), and
\(F_{j+2}=F_{j+1}+F_j\).  A binary word
\(\omega\in\{0,1\}^m\) has the raw Fibonacci value
\[
 N_m(\omega)=\sum_{j=1}^m\omega_jF_{j+1}.
\]
We fold this value modulo \(F_{m+2}\) and represent the resulting visible
value by its legal Zeckendorf word.  If \(X_m\) is the legal visible window,
the fiber multiplicity of \(x\in X_m\) is denoted by \(d_m(x)\).  The central
finite problem is to determine the complete spectrum
\(\{d_m(x):x\in X_m\}\), not only its total mass or an asymptotic moment.

The answer begins with two pointwise identities.  The first uses an affine
permutation modulo \(F_{m+2}\) to identify every fiber with a coefficient of
a finite Fibonacci subset-sum polynomial.  That coefficient is, in turn, a
difference of two values of the classical Fibonacci partition function.  The
second identity lists the fiber spectrum directly as the partition function
on two consecutive standard Fibonacci layers.  These correspondences are
exact at each \(m\), including endpoints and the single possible overflow;
no limiting normalization or transducer is needed.

Once the two-layer identity is established, the extensive theory of the
Fibonacci partition function becomes available.  We keep a strict
distinction between transferred information and finite-window conclusions.
The formulas for the largest partition multiplicities and their maximizing
integers are due to Koc\'abov\'a, Mas\'akov\'a, and Pelantov\'a
\cite{KocabovaMasakovaPelantova2005}; here they are transported through the
exact interval identity, with all Fibonacci conventions and boundary cases
checked.  Likewise, the all-real moment pressure and its first-order
transition are the golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution spectrum of
Lau--Ngai, Feng--Olivier, and Feng
\cite{LauNgai1998,FengOlivier2003,Feng2005}.  The pressure is recovered in
the present coordinates because it is needed to formulate the local and
large-deviation questions, but the recovered phase diagram is not one of the
principal claims.

The finite-window results occur below that imported pressure.  At fixed
multiplicity the spectrum stabilizes exactly after a sharp finite layer.
In the frozen range, unnormalized negative moments converge, and at the
critical tilt the Gibbs measure spreads uniformly over generator cost.  The
limiting log multiplicity and normalized cost lie on a coexistence segment.
For a uniform visible state, the pressure corner creates an interval of
nonexposed slopes.  Standard G\"artner--Ellis theory gives the upper bound
and the lower bound at exposed slopes, but not on that interval.  An explicit
orbit map fills the unused part of a target Fibonacci layer while preserving
multiplicity.  It yields the missing local lower bounds and hence a full
large deviation principle.  Marking generator cost leads to a joint rate
function with an affine two-dimensional coexistence face.

\subsection{Exact finite-window correspondences}

Let \(R(n)\) be the number of partitions of \(n\) into distinct members of
\(F_2,F_3,\ldots\), and put \(R(n)=0\) for \(n<0\).  Define
\[
 R^\dagger(n)=R(n)+R(n-1),
 \qquad
 \widetilde d_m(n)=[z^n]\prod_{j=1}^m(1+z^{F_j}).
\]
For \(0\le n<F_{m+2}\), let
\[
 \pi_m(n)\equiv F_{m+1}n+F_{m+1}-1\pmod{F_{m+2}}.
\]

\begin{theoremA}[Pointwise affine correspondence]
For every \(m\ge1\), the map \(\pi_m\) is a permutation of
\(\mathbb Z/F_{m+2}\mathbb Z\), and
\[
 d_m^\#(\pi_m(n))
 =\widetilde d_m(n)
 =R^\dagger(n)-R^\dagger(n-F_{m+1})
 \qquad(0\le n<F_{m+2}).
\]
Here \(d_m^\#\) is the residue-indexed form of the fiber multiplicity.
\end{theoremA}

This is the combined content of
\Cref{thm:affine-transfer,cor:coefficient-spectrum,thm:partition-difference}.
The proof starts with Fourier inversion for the residue fibers, uses the
exact congruence \(F_{m+1}F_j\pmod{F_{m+2}}\), and then proves the
partition-difference identity by a boundary-sensitive decomposition.  The
result is pointwise; equality of moment sums is only a corollary.

The second description uses the standard layers
\[
 \mathcal I_j=[F_{j+1}-1,F_{j+2}-1).
\]

\begin{theoremB}[Two-layer identity]
For every \(m\ge1\),
\[
 \{d_m(x):x\in X_m\}
 =\{R(n):n\in\mathcal I_m\sqcup\mathcal I_{m+1}\}
\]
as multisets.  More explicitly, for \(0\le r<F_{m+2}\),
\[
 d_m^\#(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 R(F_{m+2}+r),&0\le r\le F_{m+1}-2,\\
 R(r),&F_{m+1}-1\le r<F_{m+2}.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{theoremB}

The proof is \Cref{thm:fiber-partition-interval}.  It also shows why two
layers, rather than one asymptotic layer, are intrinsic to the fold.  As a
contextual consequence, the known extremal classification transfers to the
finite window.  If
\(D_m=\max_{x\in X_m}d_m(x)\), then
\[
 D_0=D_1=1,
 \qquad D_{2k}=F_{k+2},
 \qquad D_{2k+1}=2F_{k+1},
\]
with the ranges and exceptional cases stated in
\Cref{thm:unconditional-extremal-fibers}.  The maximizing residues and the
recurrence \(D_m=D_{m-2}+D_{m-4}\) is a transferred result, not an independent
extremal theorems about the underlying partition function.

\subsection{Local laws and the pressure input}

For a real tilt \(t\), put
\[
 S_t(m)=\sum_{x\in X_m}d_m(x)^t,
 \qquad
 P(t)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log S_t(m).
\]
If \(\tau_\mu(t)\) denotes the \(L^q\)-spectrum of the golden-ratio
Bernoulli convolution in the interval-length normalization, then its level
masses are \(2^{-m}\) times the Fibonacci representation counts and the net
scale is \(\varphi^{-m}\).  Thus the exact exponential-rate dictionary is
\begin{equation}
 P(t)=t\log2-\tau_\mu(t)\log\varphi.
 \label{eq:erdos-pressure-dictionary}
\end{equation}
The existence and phase diagram of \(P\) agree, under this dictionary, with
the published golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution \(L^q\)-spectrum.  In particular, there is
a unique \(\sigma_0>2\) satisfying
\[
 \frac{\zeta(\sigma_0-1)}{\zeta(\sigma_0)}=2,
\]
and
\[
 P(t)=0\quad(t\le-\sigma_0),
\]
while \(P\) is positive, analytic, and strictly convex for
\(t>-\sigma_0\).  The one-sided slopes at the corner are \(0\) and
\[
 v_c=\frac{\displaystyle
  \sum_{q\ge2}\sum_{\substack{1\le p<q\\(p,q)=1}}
       q^{-\sigma_0}\log q}
 {\displaystyle
  \sum_{q\ge2}\sum_{\substack{1\le p<q\\(p,q)=1}}
       c(p/q)q^{-\sigma_0}}>0.
\]
The continued-fraction cost \(c(p/q)\) and its Weinstein renewal role are
defined in \Cref{prop:weighted-generator-renewal}.  The recovery in
\Cref{thm:all-real-pressure} fixes conventions and proves the exact root
equation needed below; it does not claim priority for the spectrum.

Let \(\Psi(k)\) be Weinstein's number of generating orbits at multiplicity
level \(k\), and set
\(C_m(k)=\card{\{x\in X_m:d_m(x)=k\}}\).
The finite-window local statement is exact:
\[
 C_m(1)=2,
 \qquad C_m(k)\le4\Psi(k),
 \qquad C_m(k)=4\Psi(k)\quad(m\ge2k,\ k\ge2).
\]
This is \Cref{thm:local-fiber-spectrum}.  It includes the small levels and
half-open endpoints that are invisible at exponential scale.

For \(s>\sigma_0\), \Cref{thm:spectral-partition-function} gives
\[
 S_{-s}(m)\longrightarrow
 \mathcal Z(s)=\frac4{2-\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s)}-2.
\]
The convergence range is exact, and \(\mathcal Z\) has a simple pole at
\(\sigma_0\).  The associated fixed-level Gibbs laws and logarithmic moments
are described in \Cref{thm:critical-gibbs-spectrum}.  These are local and
unnormalized statements that the pressure alone does not supply.

At the endpoint, let
\[
 \mu_C=\sum_{q\ge2}\sum_{\substack{1\le p<q\\(p,q)=1}}
 c(p/q)q^{-\sigma_0}.
\]
For a state \(x\) of multiplicity greater than two, let \(\ell_m(x)\) be the
cost of the Weinstein generator of its orbit, with the bounded low-level
states assigned cost zero.  Under the Gibbs law
\[
 \widehat Q_m(x)=\frac{d_m(x)^{-\sigma_0}}{S_{-\sigma_0}(m)},
\]
the critical finite-window theorem states
\begin{equation}
 S_{-\sigma_0}(m)\sim\frac{4m}{\mu_C},
 \qquad
 \left(\frac{\log d_m(\widehat{\mathbf X}_m)}m,
       \frac{\ell_m(\widehat{\mathbf X}_m)}m\right)
 \xrightarrow{\mathrm d}(v_cU,U),
 \label{eq:introduction-critical-coexistence}
\end{equation}
where \(U\) is uniform on \([0,1]\); see
\Cref{thm:critical-finite-window-gibbs}.  The factor \(4\) is the exact
two-layer orbit weight away from the active boundary.

\subsection{Large deviations across the corner}

Let \(\mathbf X_m\) be uniform on \(X_m\) and put
\[
 Y_m=\frac1m\log d_m(\mathbf X_m),
 \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
 \qquad \alpha_+=\frac12\log\varphi.
\]

\begin{theoremC}[Full finite-window large deviations]
The sequence \((Y_m)\) satisfies a full large deviation principle with
speed \(m\) and good rate function
\[
 I(\alpha)=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}
 \{t\alpha-P(t)+\log\varphi\}.
\]
Its effective domain is \([0,\alpha_+]\), and
\[
 I(\alpha)=\log\varphi-\sigma_0\alpha
 \qquad(0\le\alpha\le v_c).
\]
In particular, the lower bound holds at every nonexposed slope in
\((0,v_c)\).
\end{theoremC}

This is \Cref{thm:full-fiber-ldp}.  The upper bound follows from the limiting
logarithmic moment generating function and compact support.  For an exposed
slope \(v=P'(t)>v_c\), exponential tilting provides a family of source
generators.  To reach a target slope \(\alpha<v\), the orbit map shifts each
source to a larger target layer without changing its multiplicity.  The two
orbit parities fill every sufficiently large target layer, the map is
injective by freeness, and its loss in exponential count is exactly the
scaling factor \(\alpha/v\).  Sending \(t\) down to the corner yields the
affine rate on \([0,v_c]\).  This is the step not provided by a direct
G\"artner--Ellis application.

The cost mark produces a genuinely two-dimensional statement.  On a uniform
point \(\mathbf N_m\) in one standard Fibonacci layer, let
\[
 B_m^R=\frac1m\ell_m^R(\mathbf N_m),
 \qquad
 Y_m^R=\frac1m\log R(\mathbf N_m).
\]

\begin{theoremD}[Joint cost--multiplicity large deviations]
The vectors \((B_m^R,Y_m^R)\) satisfy a full large deviation principle with
speed \(m\).  Their good rate function is
\[
 J(\beta,\alpha)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1-\beta)\log\varphi+\beta I(\alpha/\beta),
  &0<\beta\le1,\ 0\le\alpha\le\beta\alpha_+,\\
 \log\varphi,&(\beta,\alpha)=(0,0),\\
 +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Its coexistence face is
\[
 J(\beta,\alpha)=\log\varphi-\sigma_0\alpha
 \qquad(0\le\beta\le1,\ 0\le\alpha\le\beta v_c).
\]
\end{theoremD}

The proof is \Cref{thm:joint-cost-reward-ldp}.  Fixed-cost tilting handles
the strictly convex region.  On the affine face, an exact suffix of any
sufficiently large remaining cost is built from at most two generator
letters and has only logarithmic reward.  Appending it is injective in the
free monoid, so it changes normalized cost without changing the desired
exponential reward count.  This fills the nonexposed two-dimensional region.

\subsection{Contribution boundary and organization}

The pointwise affine correspondence, partition-difference formula,
two-layer identity, exact local stabilization, finite-window critical law,
nonexposed-slope orbit filling, and joint affine rate face are established in
this article.  The pressure phase diagram is imported from the
golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution literature and translated into the
present normalization.  The extremal values and maximizing integers of the
ordinary Fibonacci partition function are also imported; only their exact
finite-window transfer and the resulting residue list are established here.
The weighted Weinstein renewal identity is a direct consequence of his
published free-generator coordinates, with the layer and endpoint weights
proved in the conventions used here.

A companion manuscript by the same authors, \emph{Brocot condensation and
critical Fibonacci renewal}, proves a total-variation theorem for
denominator-weighted continued fractions and derives a sharp critical cost
tail and fractional renewal correction.  This article does not use the
total-variation theorem or the fractional correction.  Its critical
finite-window law requires only the critical probability normalization,
finite mean, and the elementary lattice renewal theorem, all verified here.

\Cref{sec:preliminaries} defines the finite fold and proves the residue
description.  \Cref{sec:residue-affine} proves the Fourier, affine, and
partition-difference identities.  \Cref{thm:fiber-partition-interval} and
the surrounding section establish the two-layer model and record the
subordinate extremal transfer and pressure conventions.  The local spectrum,
renewal normalization, critical law, and full finite-window LDP follow in
\Cref{sec:local-spectrum,thm:all-real-pressure,thm:full-fiber-ldp}.
The one-layer and joint marked results are collected in
\Cref{sec:standard-thermodynamics}.  Conditional arithmetic and integer
moment consequences are placed in the separately compiled supplement.

\section{Finite-window fibers}\label{sec:preliminaries}

Throughout, the Fibonacci numbers are indexed by
\[
  F_0=0,
  \qquad
  F_1=F_2=1,
  \qquad
  F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n
  \qquad (n\ge 0).
\]

\subsection{Stable words and the residue model}

\begin{definition}[Stable words and visible values]
\label{def:stable-words}
For \(m\ge 0\), let
\[
  \Omega_m:=\{0,1\}^m,
  \qquad
  X_m:=\{x\in\Omega_m:\ x_ix_{i+1}=0\text{ for }1\le i<m\}.
\]
For \(x\in X_m\), define
\[
  V_m(x):=\sum_{j=1}^m x_jF_{j+1}.
\]
For \(\omega=\omega_1\cdots \omega_m\in\Omega_m\), define
\[
  N_m(\omega):=\sum_{j=1}^m \omega_jF_{j+1}.
\]
Thus \(\Omega_0=X_0=\{\varepsilon\}\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the empty word,
and \(V_0(\varepsilon)=N_0(\varepsilon)=0\).
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Visible values are complete]
\label{prop:Vm-bijection}
For every \(m\ge 0\), the map
\[
  V_m\colon X_m\longrightarrow \{0,1,\dots,F_{m+2}-1\}
\]
is a bijection.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The zero word maps to \(0\), so it remains to treat
\(n\in\{1,\dots,F_{m+2}-1\}\).  By Zeckendorf's theorem
\cite{Zeckendorf1972}, \(n\) has a unique
expansion as a sum of nonconsecutive Fibonacci numbers.  Because
\(n<F_{m+2}\), that expansion cannot use the summand \(F_{m+2}\) or any larger
Fibonacci number; therefore it uses only the weights \(F_2,\dots,F_{m+1}\),
and hence determines a unique word \(x\in X_m\) with \(V_m(x)=n\).
Conversely every \(x\in X_m\) is a stable expansion in those same weights, so
\(V_m(x)\in\{0,\dots,F_{m+2}-1\}\).  Thus \(V_m\) is bijective.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Finite-window fold]
\label{def:fold-map}
For \(m\ge 0\), define
\[
  \Fold_m(\omega):=
  V_m^{-1}\bigl(N_m(\omega)\bmod F_{m+2}\bigr),
  \qquad \omega\in\Omega_m.
\]
For \(x\in X_m\), define the fiber multiplicity
\[
  d_m(x):=\card{\Fold_m^{-1}(x)}.
\]
In particular, \(\Fold_0(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\) and
\(d_0(\varepsilon)=1\).
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Single overflow]
\label{prop:single-overflow}
For every \(m\ge0\) and every \(\omega\in\Omega_m\),
\[
  N_m(\omega)\le \sum_{j=1}^m F_{j+1}=F_{m+3}-2<2F_{m+2}.
\]
Hence there exist unique integers \(b\in\{0,1\}\) and \(r\in[0,F_{m+2})\) such
that
\[
  N_m(\omega)=bF_{m+2}+r,
\]
and
\[
  \Fold_m(\omega)=V_m^{-1}(r).
\]
Equivalently, there is a unique overflow bit \(b_m(\omega)\in\{0,1\}\) such
that
\[
  N_m(\omega)=V_m(\Fold_m(\omega))+b_m(\omega)F_{m+2}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The Fibonacci identity
\(\sum_{j=1}^m F_{j+1}=F_{m+3}-2\) is standard, and
\(F_{m+3}-2<F_{m+3}-1<F_{m+3}=F_{m+2}+F_{m+1}<2F_{m+2}\).  The displayed
formula for \(\Fold_m\) is simply the definition.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Operational meaning of the fold]
\label{rem:prefix-normalization}
Because only one overflow can occur, the finite-window fold agrees with
computing the full Zeckendorf expansion of \(N_m(\omega)\) and deleting the
possible leading \(F_{m+2}\)-digit.
The residue definition is the useful one for exact fiber analysis.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Residue characterization of fibers]
\label{cor:residue-characterization}
For \(x\in X_m\), write \(r_x:=V_m(x)\).  Then
\[
  \Fold_m(\omega)=x
  \iff
  N_m(\omega)\equiv r_x \pmod{F_{m+2}}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By definition,
\(\Fold_m(\omega)=V_m^{-1}(N_m(\omega)\bmod F_{m+2})\), and \(V_m\) is
bijective by \Cref{prop:Vm-bijection}.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Notation used throughout the paper.  The letter \(q\) is reserved
for a nonnegative integer moment order, whereas \(t\) denotes a real tilt.}
\label{tab:notation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
\(\Omega_m\), \(X_m\) & raw binary words and legal visible words \\
\(\Fold_m\) & residue-defined finite-window fold \\
\(d_m(x)\), \(d_m^\#(r)\) & fiber multiplicity, indexed by a word or residue \\
\(\widetilde d_m(n)\) & coefficient of \(\prod_{j=1}^m(1+z^{F_j})\) \\
\(R(n)\), \(R^\dagger(n)\) & ordinary and indexed Fibonacci partition counts \\
\(S_q(m)\), \(S_t(m)\) & integer-order moment and real-tilt sum \\
\(T_q^\dagger(N)\) & indexed partition power sum below \(N\) \\
\(D_m\) & largest fiber multiplicity \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Thermodynamics of the Fibonacci partition function}
\label{sec:standard-thermodynamics}

The renewal identity was derived from Weinstein's standard Fibonacci
partition function before it was transferred to the finite-window fold.  We
now state its one-layer consequences intrinsically.  This removes the bespoke
fold from the probabilistic conclusions.

For \(m\ge1\), recall
\[
 \mathcal I_m=[F_{m+1}-1,F_{m+2}-1)
\]
and define
\[
 Z_m^R(t):=\sum_{n\in\mathcal I_m}R(n)^t
 \qquad(t\in\RR).
\]
If \(\mathbf N_m\) is uniform on \(\mathcal I_m\), put
\[
 Y_m^R:=\frac1m\log R(\mathbf N_m).
\]

\begin{theorem}[One-layer Fibonacci partition thermodynamics]
\label{thm:standard-fibonacci-thermodynamics}
For every \(t\in\RR\),
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log Z_m^R(t)=P(t),
 \label{eq:standard-layer-pressure}
\end{equation}
where \(P\) is the pressure in \Cref{thm:all-real-pressure}.  Thus the
one-layer pressure is zero on \((-\infty,-\sigma_0]\), is positive, real
analytic, and strictly convex on \((-\sigma_0,\infty)\), and has the
one-sided derivatives in \eqref{eq:critical-pressure-slopes}.

For \(s>\sigma_0\), the unnormalized sums satisfy
\begin{equation}
 Z_m^R(-s)\longrightarrow
 \mathcal Z_R(s):=
 \frac2{2-\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s)}-1.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-frozen-limit}
\end{equation}
At the critical tilt,
\begin{equation}
 Z_m^R(-\sigma_0)\sim\frac{2m}{\mu_C}.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-critical-size}
\end{equation}

For \(n\in\mathcal I_m\) with \(R(n)>2\), let \(g(n)\) be the generating
number of its Weinstein orbit and put \(\ell_m^R(n)=L(g(n))\); set
\(\ell_m^R(n)=0\) when \(R(n)\le2\).  Let \(\widehat{\mathbf N}_m\) have the
critical Gibbs law
\[
 \Pr\{\widehat{\mathbf N}_m=n\}
 =\frac{R(n)^{-\sigma_0}}{Z_m^R(-\sigma_0)}
 \qquad(n\in\mathcal I_m).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left(
  \frac1m\log R(\widehat{\mathbf N}_m),
  \frac1m\ell_m^R(\widehat{\mathbf N}_m)
 \right)
 \xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{\mathrm d}(v_cU,U),
 \label{eq:standard-layer-critical-gibbs}
\end{equation}
where \(U\) is uniform on \([0,1]\).

Finally, \((Y_m^R)\) satisfies a full large deviation principle with speed
\(m\) and the good rate function
\begin{equation}
 I(\alpha)=\sup_{t\in\RR}
 \{t\alpha-P(t)+\log\varphi\}.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-ldp-rate}
\end{equation}
Its effective domain is \([0,\alpha_+]\), where
\(\alpha_+=\tfrac12\log\varphi\), and
\[
 I(\alpha)=\log\varphi-\sigma_0\alpha
 \qquad(0\le\alpha\le v_c).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put \(H_m(s)=\sum_{j=0}^m u_j(s)\).  The exact one-layer renewal identity
\eqref{eq:weighted-layer-renewal} says
\begin{equation}
 Z_m^R(-s)=2H_{m-1}(s)+u_m(s)-1.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-renewal}
\end{equation}
The proof of \Cref{thm:all-real-pressure} established
\[
 \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log u_m(s)
 =\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log H_m(s)
 =P(-s).
\]
Since \(u_m(s)\le Z_m^R(-s)\le3H_m(s)\), this proves
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-pressure}.

If \(s>\sigma_0\), then \(U_s(1)=\sum_{j\ge0}u_j(s)<\infty\), so
\(u_m(s)\to0\).  Equations
\eqref{eq:weighted-renewal-generating-function} and
\eqref{eq:weighted-renewal-at-one} give
\[
 U_s(1)=\frac1{1-B_s(1)}
 =\frac1{2-\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s)}.
\]
Letting \(m\to\infty\) in \eqref{eq:standard-layer-renewal} proves
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-frozen-limit}.  At \(s=\sigma_0\), the arithmetic
renewal theorem used in \Cref{thm:critical-finite-window-gibbs} gives
\(u_m(\sigma_0)\to1/\mu_C\).  Ces\`aro summation in
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-renewal} proves
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-critical-size}.

We next retain the generating cost.  The four orbit branches displayed above
\eqref{eq:marked-microcanonical-count} show that a generator of cost \(c\)
contributes two points to \(\mathcal I_m\) if \(c<m\), one if \(c=m\), and
none if \(c>m\).  Thus the one-layer boundary weight is
\[
 K_m^R(c)=
 \begin{cases}
  2,&c<m,\\
  1,&c=m,\\
  0,&c>m.
 \end{cases}
\]
With the marked renewal measure \(\mathcal U\) defined before
\eqref{eq:marked-microcanonical-count}, the same free-monoid bijection gives,
for every Borel set
\(B\subset\mathbb R\times(\log2,\infty)\),
\begin{equation}
 \card{\{n\in\mathcal I_m:
   (\ell_m^R(n),\log R(n))\in B\}}
 =\int_B K_m^R(c)e^{\sigma_0h}\,\mathcal U(dc,dh).
 \label{eq:standard-layer-marked-count}
\end{equation}
The points with \(R(n)\le2\) have bounded total critical weight, uniformly in
\(m\), by the uniform layer-count lemma.

For every bounded continuous \(f\) on \([0,1]\), the arithmetic renewal
theorem and a Riemann-sum argument give
\[
 \frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_j(\sigma_0)f(j/m)
 \longrightarrow\frac1{\mu_C}\int_0^1f(y)\,dy.
\]
After multiplication of \eqref{eq:standard-layer-marked-count} by
\(e^{-\sigma_0h}\), the weights are two for \(j<m\) and one at \(j=m\).
Together with \eqref{eq:standard-layer-critical-size}, this proves
\[
 \frac{\ell_m^R(\widehat{\mathbf N}_m)}m
 \xrightarrow{\mathrm d}U.
\]
For the reward coordinate, the critical renewal increments
\((C_i,H_i)\) satisfy
\[
 \frac{H_1+\cdots+H_r}{C_1+\cdots+C_r}
 \longrightarrow\frac{\mu_H}{\mu_C}=v_c
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Every cost increment is at least three.  Consequently the number of renewal
epochs with total cost at most \(m\) and reward-to-cost ratio outside a fixed
\(\delta\)-neighborhood of \(v_c\) is \(o(m)\), pathwise and, by bounded
convergence after division by \(m\), in expectation.  Since \(K_m^R\le2\),
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-marked-count} and
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-critical-size} imply
\[
 \frac1m\log R(\widehat{\mathbf N}_m)
 -v_c\frac{\ell_m^R(\widehat{\mathbf N}_m)}m
 \xrightarrow{\Pr}0.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:standard-layer-critical-gibbs}.

It remains to prove the full LDP, in particular the lower bound at the
nonexposed slopes.  The layer has
\(\card{\mathcal I_m}=F_m\), and hence
\[
 \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log\card{\mathcal I_m}=\log\varphi.
\]
Equation \eqref{eq:standard-layer-pressure} therefore gives the limiting
logarithmic moment generating function
\[
 \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m
 \log\mathbb E e^{tmY_m^R}=P(t)-\log\varphi.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-log-mgf}
\]
The translated extremal theorem in the Fibonacci-convention lemma gives
\[
 \max_{n\in\mathcal I_m}\frac1m\log R(n)
 \longrightarrow\alpha_+.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-maximum}
\]
Indeed, the two shifted endpoints have partition value one, so they do not
change the maximum on the intervening Fibonacci block.  Thus the variables
are exponentially tight, and the G\"artner--Ellis upper bound gives the
required upper bound for closed sets.

For the lower bound, first let \(t>t_c=-\sigma_0\), write
\(v=P'(t)>v_c\), and
tilt the uniform law on \(\mathcal I_n\) by \(R(k)^t\).  Analyticity of \(P\)
and the exponential Markov inequality applied to
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-pressure} show that this tilted law assigns
exponentially vanishing mass to
\[
 \left\{k\in\mathcal I_n:
   \left|n^{-1}\log R(k)-v\right|\ge\delta\right\}.
\]
Consequently, if
\[
 A_n^R(v,\delta)
 :=\card{\{k\in\mathcal I_n:
 |n^{-1}\log R(k)-v|<\delta\}},
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log A_n^R(v,\delta)
 \ge P(t)-tv-|t|\delta.
 \label{eq:standard-layer-exposed-source}
\end{equation}

For large \(n\), every point counted here has multiplicity greater than two.
Each generating orbit contributes at most two points to \(\mathcal I_n\).
Keeping one generator from each represented orbit therefore produces a set
\(\mathcal G_n^R\) with
\[
 \card{\mathcal G_n^R}\ge\tfrac12A_n^R(v,\delta),
 \qquad L(g)\le n\quad(g\in\mathcal G_n^R),
\]
and \(n^{-1}\log R(g)\in(v-\delta,v+\delta)\).

Fix \(0<\alpha<\alpha_+\).  Choose \(t>t_c\) so that
\(v=P'(t)>\alpha\): any \(t>t_c\) works when \(\alpha\le v_c\), while for
\(\alpha>v_c\) take \(t>t_\alpha\), where
\(P'(t_\alpha)=\alpha\).  Only after this choice set
\(\rho=\alpha/v<1\), and put
\(n_m=\lfloor\rho m\rfloor\).  For \(g\in\mathcal G_{n_m}^R\), define
\[
 z_m(g)=
 \begin{cases}
  [a]g,&m-L(g)=2a,\\
  [a]\tau g,&m-L(g)=2a+1.
 \end{cases}
\]
The orbit formulas give \(L(z_m(g))=m\) and
\(R(z_m(g))=R(g)\), so \(z_m(g)\in\mathcal I_m\).  Freeness makes this map
injective.  From \eqref{eq:standard-layer-exposed-source}, first letting
\(\delta\downarrow0\), we obtain the local counting lower bound
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\liminf_{m\to\infty}\frac1m
 \log A_m^R(\alpha,\varepsilon)
 \ge\frac{\alpha}{v}\bigl(P(t)-tv\bigr).
 \label{eq:standard-layer-orbit-filling}
\end{equation}

If \(0<\alpha\le v_c\), let \(t\downarrow t_c\) through the choices above in
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-orbit-filling}; then \(v\downarrow v_c\) and the
right side tends to \(\sigma_0\alpha\).  If
\(v_c<\alpha<\alpha_+\), use the \(t_\alpha\) just defined and let
\(t\downarrow t_\alpha\) through values with
\(P'(t)>\alpha\).  The right side then tends to
\(P(t_\alpha)-t_\alpha\alpha\).  In both cases this is
\(\log\varphi-I(\alpha)\).  Division by
\(\card{\mathcal I_m}=F_m\) proves the LDP lower bound at every interior
point of the effective domain.

The effective domain and the affine formula follow from the same convex-dual
calculation as in \Cref{thm:full-fiber-ldp}, since the pressure is the same.
At \(0\), the left endpoint \(F_{m+1}-1\) has \(R=1\) and supplies the lower
bound directly.  For the other boundary passage, let \(G\) be open and contain
\(a\in[0,\alpha_+]\).  Choose interior points \(a_j\to a\) (at
\(a=\alpha_+\), take \(a_j\uparrow\alpha_+\)).  Relative continuity of the
explicit finite rate gives \(I(a_j)\to I(a)\), while openness gives intervals
about \(a_j\) contained in \(G\) for large \(j\).  The interior local bound,
followed by \(j\to\infty\), gives the lower bound at \(a\).  Taking the
infimum over \(G\cap[0,\alpha_+]\) completes the full LDP.
\end{proof}

For the same uniform point \(\mathbf N_m\), retain the generating cost by
putting
\[
 B_m^R:=\frac1m\ell_m^R(\mathbf N_m).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Joint generation-cost and multiplicity large deviations]
\label{thm:joint-cost-reward-ldp}
The vectors \((B_m^R,Y_m^R)\) satisfy a full large deviation principle on
\(\mathbb R^2\) with speed \(m\).  Their limiting logarithmic moment generating
function is
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda(a,t)=\max\{0,a+P(t)\}-\log\varphi
 \qquad(a,t\in\mathbb R).
 \label{eq:joint-cost-reward-log-mgf}
\end{equation}
The good rate function is
\begin{equation}
 J(\beta,\alpha)=
 \begin{cases}
  (1-\beta)\log\varphi+\beta I(\alpha/\beta),
   &0<\beta\le1,\quad 0\le\alpha\le\beta\alpha_+,\\
  \log\varphi,&(\beta,\alpha)=(0,0),\\
  +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:joint-cost-reward-rate}
\end{equation}
In particular, the rate surface has the affine face
\begin{equation}
 J(\beta,\alpha)=\log\varphi-\sigma_0\alpha
 \qquad(0\le\beta\le1,\ 0\le\alpha\le\beta v_c).
 \label{eq:joint-cost-reward-flat-face}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal W_j\) be the set of nonempty free generator words of total
cost \(j\), and write \(Q(w)\) for the product of the denominators of the
letters of \(w\).  By \eqref{eq:generator-weight-length},
\begin{equation}
 u_j(-t)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W_j}Q(w)^t.
 \label{eq:fixed-cost-word-partition}
\end{equation}
The convention \(\ell_m^R=0\) at multiplicities at most two changes only a
bounded number of states.  The one-layer orbit weights in
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-marked-count} therefore give, up to a term bounded
for each fixed \((a,t)\),
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n\in\mathcal I_m}e^{a\ell_m^R(n)}R(n)^t
 =2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}e^{aj}u_j(-t)+e^{am}u_m(-t)+O_{a,t}(1).
 \label{eq:joint-cost-reward-renewal}
\end{equation}
More precisely, the bounded correction removes the level-two generator orbit
from its positive cost and records it at cost zero; the level-one endpoint is
already a cost-zero term.

The proof of \Cref{thm:all-real-pressure} established
\(\lim_{j\to\infty}j^{-1}\log u_j(-t)=P(t)\), and \(u_j(-t)>0\) for every
\(j\ge8\).  Applying these facts to the partial sum in
\eqref{eq:joint-cost-reward-renewal}, while retaining the level-one endpoint,
gives
\[
 \lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log
 \sum_{n\in\mathcal I_m}e^{a\ell_m^R(n)}R(n)^t
 =\max\{0,a+P(t)\}.
\]
Since \(\card{\mathcal I_m}=F_m\), this proves
\eqref{eq:joint-cost-reward-log-mgf}.

We next compute its convex dual.  For fixed \(t\),
\[
 \sup_{a\in\mathbb R}\{a\beta-\max(0,a+P(t))\}
 =\begin{cases}
   -\beta P(t),&0\le\beta\le1,\\
   +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\]
For \(0<\beta\le1\), subsequent optimization over \(t\) gives
\[
 \log\varphi+\beta\sup_t\{t\alpha/\beta-P(t)\}
 =(1-\beta)\log\varphi+\beta I(\alpha/\beta).
\]
At \(\beta=0\), the dual is finite only at \(\alpha=0\), where it equals
\(\log\varphi\).  The effective domain of \(I\) from
\Cref{thm:standard-fibonacci-thermodynamics} now gives exactly
\eqref{eq:joint-cost-reward-rate}.  The variables are supported in a common
compact set up to a vanishing enlargement: \(0\le B_m^R\le1\), and
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-maximum} bounds \(Y_m^R\).  Thus the
G\"artner--Ellis upper bound applies to every closed set.

It remains to prove the lower bound, because the interior points with
\(0<\beta<1\) are not exposed points of \(\Lambda\).  For any \(t>t_c\), put
\(v=P'(t)>v_c\), and on \(\mathcal W_j\) use the probability proportional to
\(Q(w)^t\).  For sufficiently small real \(s\),
\eqref{eq:fixed-cost-word-partition} and the fixed-cost pressure limit give
\[
 \limsup_{j\to\infty}\frac1j\log
 \Pr_t\left\{\left|j^{-1}\log Q(w)-v\right|\ge\delta\right\}<0.
\]
This is the same two-sided exponential Markov argument as in
\eqref{eq:standard-layer-exposed-source}.  Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{j\to\infty}\frac1j\log
 \card{\{w\in\mathcal W_j:\ |j^{-1}\log Q(w)-v|<\delta\}}
 \ge P(t)-tv-|t|\delta.
 \label{eq:fixed-cost-exposed-source}
\end{equation}

Let \(0<\beta\le1\) and suppose first that \(\alpha/\beta>v_c\).  Choose the
unique \(t>t_c\) with \(v=P'(t)=\alpha/\beta\).  Taking integers \(j_m\) with
\(j_m/m\to\beta\),
each word counted in \eqref{eq:fixed-cost-exposed-source} determines at least
one point of \(\mathcal I_m\), because a generator orbit of cost \(j_m\le m\)
meets that layer.  Freeness preserves injectivity.  Hence the local counting
exponent is at least
\(\beta(P(t)-t\alpha/\beta)\), which, after division by \(F_m\), is
\(-J(\beta,\alpha)\).  The same conclusion at \(v_c\) follows by approximation
from \(t\downarrow t_c\).

Now fix \(0<\alpha\le\beta v_c\), choose \(t>t_c\), and put
\(v=P'(t)>v_c\ge\alpha/\beta\); thus \(\alpha/v<\beta\).  Set
\[
 k_m=\left\lfloor\frac{\alpha m}{v}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad j_m=\lfloor\beta m\rfloor,
 \qquad r_m=j_m-k_m.
\]
Because \(\alpha/v<\beta\), the integer \(r_m\) tends linearly to infinity;
the two floor errors are bounded.  Every integer \(r\ge6\) is the exact cost
of a suffix of at most two letters.  For odd \(r\), take the letter \(1/q\)
with \(q=(r+1)/2\), whose cost is \(2q-1=r\).  For even \(r\), take the
ordered pair \((1/2,1/q)\) with \(q=(r-2)/2\); its cost is
\(3+(2q-1)=r\).  This includes \(r=6\), where both letters are \(1/2\), and
\(r=7\), where the one-letter construction has \(q=4\).  Repeated letters
are allowed in Weinstein's free monoid.  The suffix multiplier is at most
\(2q\), so its logarithmic reward is \(O(\log r)=o(m)\).

Append the suffix of cost \(r_m\) to every source word of cost \(k_m\) counted
in \eqref{eq:fixed-cost-exposed-source}.  Right cancellation in the free
monoid makes this map injective, and the total cost is exactly \(j_m\).  The
source reward differs from \(vk_m\) by at most \(\delta k_m\), the floor
error in \(vk_m/m\) is at most \(v/m\), and the suffix contributes \(o(1)\)
after division by \(m\).  Thus the images enter every prescribed
neighborhood of \((\beta,\alpha)\) after first choosing \(\delta\) and then
letting \(m\to\infty\).  Their local counting exponent is at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha}{v}\{P(t)-tv\}.
\]
Letting \(t\downarrow t_c=-\sigma_0\), and using \(P(t)\to0\) and
\(v\downarrow v_c\), gives the exponent \(\sigma_0\alpha\).  For
\(\alpha=0\), choose the suffix of exact cost
\(j_m=\lfloor\beta m\rfloor\) by the same construction; it has reward
\(O(\log m)=o(m)\) and gives exponent zero.  After normalization by \(F_m\),
these bounds equal the negative of
\eqref{eq:joint-cost-reward-flat-face}.  The point \((0,0)\) is supplied by
the level-one endpoint.

To formalize all remaining boundary cases, let
\[
 \mathcal D=\{(\beta,\alpha):0\le\beta\le1,
                 0\le\alpha\le\beta\alpha_+\}
\]
with its relative topology.  The explicit formula
\eqref{eq:joint-cost-reward-rate} is continuous on \(\mathcal D\).  If an
open set \(G\subset\mathbb R^2\) meets \(\mathcal D\) at a boundary point
other than \((0,0)\), choose relative-interior points
\((\beta_j,\alpha_j)\in G\cap\mathcal D\) converging to it; for the upper
edge take \(\alpha_j<\beta_j\alpha_+\), and for \(\beta=1\) take
\(\beta_j<1\).  The local bounds already proved and continuity give the
boundary lower bound after \(j\to\infty\).  Taking the infimum over
\(G\cap\mathcal D\), together with the direct point \((0,0)\), proves the
lower bound for every open set and completes the full LDP.
\end{proof}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The finite-window fold has two exact arithmetic models.  The affine residue
permutation gives a pointwise coefficient-spectrum identity and the
partition-difference formula, while the interval identity gives the complete
fiber multiset as two consecutive layers of the classical Fibonacci
partition function.  Their roles are complementary: the first resolves each
residue, and the second exposes the orbit and renewal structure.

The imported pressure describes the exponential scale but does not settle
the finite-window questions at its corner.  Exact orbit weights yield local
spectral stabilization and the critical linear partition sum.  Under the
critical Gibbs law, normalized generator cost becomes uniform and log
multiplicity follows it along the coexistence segment.  These statements
retain information that disappears after taking only logarithmic moment
growth.

The same distinction is decisive for large deviations.  The pressure corner
creates nonexposed slopes, so a convex-duality upper bound alone cannot prove
a full principle.  The generator-orbit filling construction supplies the
missing one-dimensional lower bounds.  When generator cost is marked, an
exact low-reward suffix fills the remaining cost and produces the affine
coexistence face of the joint rate surface.

The pressure phase diagram and the extremal classification remain
subordinate inputs: the former comes from the golden-ratio
Bernoulli-convolution spectrum, and the latter from the known classification
of ordinary Fibonacci partitions.  What is specific to the finite window is
the exact correspondence, the boundary-sensitive transfer, the local and
critical laws, and the completion of the lower bounds across the freezing
corner.

The companion manuscript \emph{Brocot condensation and critical Fibonacci
renewal} studies the continued-fraction context law that sharpens the
critical generator tail.  Its total-variation theorem is not used here.  In
the other direction, the finite-window identities and large deviations of
this article are not needed for the classical one-layer renewal correction.
This limited interface keeps the two arithmetic mechanisms independently
readable.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Let \(F_0=0,F_1=F_2=1\), and
\(F_{j+2}=F_{j+1}+F_j\).  A binary word
\(\omega\in\{0,1\}^m\) has the raw Fibonacci value
\[
 N_m(\omega)=\sum_{j=1}^m\omega_jF_{j+1}.
\]
We fold this value modulo \(F_{m+2}\) and represent the resulting visible
value by its legal Zeckendorf word.  If \(X_m\) is the legal visible window,
the fiber multiplicity of \(x\in X_m\) is denoted by \(d_m(x)\).  The central
finite problem is to determine the complete spectrum
\(\{d_m(x):x\in X_m\}\), not only its total mass or an asymptotic moment.

The answer begins with two pointwise identities.  The first uses an affine
permutation modulo \(F_{m+2}\) to identify every fiber with a coefficient of
a finite Fibonacci subset-sum polynomial.  That coefficient is, in turn, a
difference of two values of the classical Fibonacci partition function.  The
second identity lists the fiber spectrum directly as the partition function
on two consecutive standard Fibonacci layers.  These correspondences are
exact at each \(m\), including endpoints and the single possible overflow;
no limiting normalization or transducer is needed.

Once the two-layer identity is established, the extensive theory of the
Fibonacci partition function becomes available.  We keep a strict
distinction between transferred information and finite-window conclusions.
The formulas for the largest partition multiplicities and their maximizing
integers are due to Koc\'abov\'a, Mas\'akov\'a, and Pelantov\'a
\cite{KocabovaMasakovaPelantova2005}; here they are transported through the
exact interval identity, with all Fibonacci conventions and boundary cases
checked.  Likewise, the all-real moment pressure and its first-order
transition are the golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution spectrum of
Lau--Ngai, Feng--Olivier, and Feng
\cite{LauNgai1998,FengOlivier2003,Feng2005}.  The pressure is recovered in
the present coordinates because it is needed to formulate the local and
large-deviation questions, but the recovered phase diagram is not one of the
principal claims.

The finite-window results occur below that imported pressure.  At fixed
multiplicity the spectrum stabilizes exactly after a sharp finite layer.
In the frozen range, unnormalized negative moments converge, and at the
critical tilt the Gibbs measure spreads uniformly over generator cost.  The
limiting log multiplicity and normalized cost lie on a coexistence segment.
For a uniform visible state, the pressure corner creates an interval of
nonexposed slopes.  Standard G\"artner--Ellis theory gives the upper bound
and the lower bound at exposed slopes, but not on that interval.  An explicit
orbit map fills the unused part of a target Fibonacci layer while preserving
multiplicity.  It yields the missing local lower bounds and hence a full
large deviation principle.  Marking generator cost leads to a joint rate
function with an affine two-dimensional coexistence face.

\subsection{Exact finite-window correspondences}

Let \(R(n)\) be the number of partitions of \(n\) into distinct members of
\(F_2,F_3,\ldots\), and put \(R(n)=0\) for \(n<0\).  Define
\[
 R^\dagger(n)=R(n)+R(n-1),
 \qquad
 \widetilde d_m(n)=[z^n]\prod_{j=1}^m(1+z^{F_j}).
\]
For \(0\le n<F_{m+2}\), let
\[
 \pi_m(n)\equiv F_{m+1}n+F_{m+1}-1\pmod{F_{m+2}}.
\]

\begin{theoremA}[Pointwise affine correspondence]
For every \(m\ge1\), the map \(\pi_m\) is a permutation of
\(\mathbb Z/F_{m+2}\mathbb Z\), and
\[
 d_m^\#(\pi_m(n))
 =\widetilde d_m(n)
 =R^\dagger(n)-R^\dagger(n-F_{m+1})
 \qquad(0\le n<F_{m+2}).
\]
Here \(d_m^\#\) is the residue-indexed form of the fiber multiplicity.
\end{theoremA}

This is the combined content of
\Cref{thm:affine-transfer,cor:coefficient-spectrum,thm:partition-difference}.
The proof starts with Fourier inversion for the residue fibers, uses the
exact congruence \(F_{m+1}F_j\pmod{F_{m+2}}\), and then proves the
partition-difference identity by a boundary-sensitive decomposition.  The
result is pointwise; equality of moment sums is only a corollary.

The second description uses the standard layers
\[
 \mathcal I_j=[F_{j+1}-1,F_{j+2}-1).
\]

\begin{theoremB}[Two-layer identity]
For every \(m\ge1\),
\[
 \{d_m(x):x\in X_m\}
 =\{R(n):n\in\mathcal I_m\sqcup\mathcal I_{m+1}\}
\]
as multisets.  More explicitly, for \(0\le r<F_{m+2}\),
\[
 d_m^\#(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 R(F_{m+2}+r),&0\le r\le F_{m+1}-2,\\
 R(r),&F_{m+1}-1\le r<F_{m+2}.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{theoremB}

The proof is \Cref{thm:fiber-partition-interval}.  It also shows why two
layers, rather than one asymptotic layer, are intrinsic to the fold.  As a
contextual consequence, the known extremal classification transfers to the
finite window.  If
\(D_m=\max_{x\in X_m}d_m(x)\), then
\[
 D_0=D_1=1,
 \qquad D_{2k}=F_{k+2},
 \qquad D_{2k+1}=2F_{k+1},
\]
with the ranges and exceptional cases stated in
\Cref{thm:unconditional-extremal-fibers}.  The maximizing residues and the
recurrence \(D_m=D_{m-2}+D_{m-4}\) is a transferred result, not an independent
extremal theorems about the underlying partition function.

\subsection{Local laws and the pressure input}

For a real tilt \(t\), put
\[
 S_t(m)=\sum_{x\in X_m}d_m(x)^t,
 \qquad
 P(t)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac1m\log S_t(m).
\]
If \(\tau_\mu(t)\) denotes the \(L^q\)-spectrum of the golden-ratio
Bernoulli convolution in the interval-length normalization, then its level
masses are \(2^{-m}\) times the Fibonacci representation counts and the net
scale is \(\varphi^{-m}\).  Thus the exact exponential-rate dictionary is
\begin{equation}
 P(t)=t\log2-\tau_\mu(t)\log\varphi.
 \label{eq:erdos-pressure-dictionary}
\end{equation}
The existence and phase diagram of \(P\) agree, under this dictionary, with
the published golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution \(L^q\)-spectrum.  In particular, there is
a unique \(\sigma_0>2\) satisfying
\[
 \frac{\zeta(\sigma_0-1)}{\zeta(\sigma_0)}=2,
\]
and
\[
 P(t)=0\quad(t\le-\sigma_0),
\]
while \(P\) is positive, analytic, and strictly convex for
\(t>-\sigma_0\).  The one-sided slopes at the corner are \(0\) and
\[
 v_c=\frac{\displaystyle
  \sum_{q\ge2}\sum_{\substack{1\le p<q\\(p,q)=1}}
       q^{-\sigma_0}\log q}
 {\displaystyle
  \sum_{q\ge2}\sum_{\substack{1\le p<q\\(p,q)=1}}
       c(p/q)q^{-\sigma_0}}>0.
\]
The continued-fraction cost \(c(p/q)\) and its Weinstein renewal role are
defined in \Cref{prop:weighted-generator-renewal}.  The recovery in
\Cref{thm:all-real-pressure} fixes conventions and proves the exact root
equation needed below; it does not claim priority for the spectrum.

Let \(\Psi(k)\) be Weinstein's number of generating orbits at multiplicity
level \(k\), and set
\(C_m(k)=\card{\{x\in X_m:d_m(x)=k\}}\).
The finite-window local statement is exact:
\[
 C_m(1)=2,
 \qquad C_m(k)\le4\Psi(k),
 \qquad C_m(k)=4\Psi(k)\quad(m\ge2k,\ k\ge2).
\]
This is \Cref{thm:local-fiber-spectrum}.  It includes the small levels and
half-open endpoints that are invisible at exponential scale.

For \(s>\sigma_0\), \Cref{thm:spectral-partition-function} gives
\[
 S_{-s}(m)\longrightarrow
 \mathcal Z(s)=\frac4{2-\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s)}-2.
\]
The convergence range is exact, and \(\mathcal Z\) has a simple pole at
\(\sigma_0\).  The associated fixed-level Gibbs laws and logarithmic moments
are described in \Cref{thm:critical-gibbs-spectrum}.  These are local and
unnormalized statements that the pressure alone does not supply.

At the endpoint, let
\[
 \mu_C=\sum_{q\ge2}\sum_{\substack{1\le p<q\\(p,q)=1}}
 c(p/q)q^{-\sigma_0}.
\]
For a state \(x\) of multiplicity greater than two, let \(\ell_m(x)\) be the
cost of the Weinstein generator of its orbit, with the bounded low-level
states assigned cost zero.  Under the Gibbs law
\[
 \widehat Q_m(x)=\frac{d_m(x)^{-\sigma_0}}{S_{-\sigma_0}(m)},
\]
the critical finite-window theorem states
\begin{equation}
 S_{-\sigma_0}(m)\sim\frac{4m}{\mu_C},
 \qquad
 \left(\frac{\log d_m(\widehat{\mathbf X}_m)}m,
       \frac{\ell_m(\widehat{\mathbf X}_m)}m\right)
 \xrightarrow{\mathrm d}(v_cU,U),
 \label{eq:introduction-critical-coexistence}
\end{equation}
where \(U\) is uniform on \([0,1]\); see
\Cref{thm:critical-finite-window-gibbs}.  The factor \(4\) is the exact
two-layer orbit weight away from the active boundary.

\subsection{Large deviations across the corner}

Let \(\mathbf X_m\) be uniform on \(X_m\) and put
\[
 Y_m=\frac1m\log d_m(\mathbf X_m),
 \qquad \varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
 \qquad \alpha_+=\frac12\log\varphi.
\]

\begin{theoremC}[Full finite-window large deviations]
The sequence \((Y_m)\) satisfies a full large deviation principle with
speed \(m\) and good rate function
\[
 I(\alpha)=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}
 \{t\alpha-P(t)+\log\varphi\}.
\]
Its effective domain is \([0,\alpha_+]\), and
\[
 I(\alpha)=\log\varphi-\sigma_0\alpha
 \qquad(0\le\alpha\le v_c).
\]
In particular, the lower bound holds at every nonexposed slope in
\((0,v_c)\).
\end{theoremC}

This is \Cref{thm:full-fiber-ldp}.  The upper bound follows from the limiting
logarithmic moment generating function and compact support.  For an exposed
slope \(v=P'(t)>v_c\), exponential tilting provides a family of source
generators.  To reach a target slope \(\alpha<v\), the orbit map shifts each
source to a larger target layer without changing its multiplicity.  The two
orbit parities fill every sufficiently large target layer, the map is
injective by freeness, and its loss in exponential count is exactly the
scaling factor \(\alpha/v\).  Sending \(t\) down to the corner yields the
affine rate on \([0,v_c]\).  This is the step not provided by a direct
G\"artner--Ellis application.

The cost mark produces a genuinely two-dimensional statement.  On a uniform
point \(\mathbf N_m\) in one standard Fibonacci layer, let
\[
 B_m^R=\frac1m\ell_m^R(\mathbf N_m),
 \qquad
 Y_m^R=\frac1m\log R(\mathbf N_m).
\]

\begin{theoremD}[Joint cost--multiplicity large deviations]
The vectors \((B_m^R,Y_m^R)\) satisfy a full large deviation principle with
speed \(m\).  Their good rate function is
\[
 J(\beta,\alpha)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1-\beta)\log\varphi+\beta I(\alpha/\beta),
  &0<\beta\le1,\ 0\le\alpha\le\beta\alpha_+,\\
 \log\varphi,&(\beta,\alpha)=(0,0),\\
 +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Its coexistence face is
\[
 J(\beta,\alpha)=\log\varphi-\sigma_0\alpha
 \qquad(0\le\beta\le1,\ 0\le\alpha\le\beta v_c).
\]
\end{theoremD}

The proof is \Cref{thm:joint-cost-reward-ldp}.  Fixed-cost tilting handles
the strictly convex region.  On the affine face, an exact suffix of any
sufficiently large remaining cost is built from at most two generator
letters and has only logarithmic reward.  Appending it is injective in the
free monoid, so it changes normalized cost without changing the desired
exponential reward count.  This fills the nonexposed two-dimensional region.

\subsection{Contribution boundary and organization}

The pointwise affine correspondence, partition-difference formula,
two-layer identity, exact local stabilization, finite-window critical law,
nonexposed-slope orbit filling, and joint affine rate face are established in
this article.  The pressure phase diagram is imported from the
golden-ratio Bernoulli-convolution literature and translated into the
present normalization.  The extremal values and maximizing integers of the
ordinary Fibonacci partition function are also imported; only their exact
finite-window transfer and the resulting residue list are established here.
The weighted Weinstein renewal identity is a direct consequence of his
published free-generator coordinates, with the layer and endpoint weights
proved in the conventions used here.

A companion manuscript by the same authors, \emph{Brocot condensation and
critical Fibonacci renewal}, proves a total-variation theorem for
denominator-weighted continued fractions and derives a sharp critical cost
tail and fractional renewal correction.  This article does not use the
total-variation theorem or the fractional correction.  Its critical
finite-window law requires only the critical probability normalization,
finite mean, and the elementary lattice renewal theorem, all verified here.

\Cref{sec:preliminaries} defines the finite fold and proves the residue
description.  \Cref{sec:residue-affine} proves the Fourier, affine, and
partition-difference identities.  \Cref{thm:fiber-partition-interval} and
the surrounding section establish the two-layer model and record the
subordinate extremal transfer and pressure conventions.  The local spectrum,
renewal normalization, critical law, and full finite-window LDP follow in
\Cref{sec:local-spectrum,thm:all-real-pressure,thm:full-fiber-ldp}.
The one-layer and joint marked results are collected in
\Cref{sec:standard-thermodynamics}.  Conditional arithmetic and integer
moment consequences are placed in the separately compiled supplement.
